speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPAIRS TO COASTGUARD SHIP "NANOOK"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a question to the Minister of Transport, and ask him whether the department has cancelled its order for the building of C.C.G.S. Nanook in the Pictou shipyard. If so, what is the reason for this action?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPAIRS TO COASTGUARD SHIP "NANOOK"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was never any order for building the ship. It is a ship which was damaged in the ice in the north this summer, and tenders were called for the repair work on it. The lowest bidder was the yard at Pictou but the cost, as revealed by the competitive tenders, is so high in relation to the two weeks of work required of this ship in the summer in the Hudson strait that it was decided to delay the work, because it can always be done later if it is found necessary to do it. But in view of the prospective use of
5982	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry the ship it was thought inadvisable to go ahead with the work at that enormous cost.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPAIRS TO COASTGUARD SHIP "NANOOK"
speechtext: As a supplementary question, in view of the high amount of unemployment in that area would the minister be prepared to reconsider the department's decision in that regard?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPAIRS TO COASTGUARD SHIP "NANOOK"
speechtext: I am very well aware and very conscious of the high unemployment in the area. That is why I was so pleased yesterday with the public announcement of the contract for building flat cars there. But the point here is that it is very difficult to justify a repair bill of that sort for two weeks' use of a ship in the summer as living quarters for the crew while working unloading freight in the north, when there are other ships available that do not require any such expenditure.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPAIRS TO COASTGUARD SHIP "NANOOK"

Would the minister consider leaving the ship there for the present?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPAIRS TO COASTGUARD SHIP "NANOOK"
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I would be very glad to do that.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Justice. Has the minister or his legal advisers finished reading and analysing Jacques Hebert's book entitled "J'aecuse les assassins de Coffin"? If so, have they come to the conclusion that a royal commission must be set up?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the high officials of the department have finished reading the book, but they are now examining the lengthy departmental file concerning the decision taken in 1956 to refuse the commutation.
There are two aspects to this question. First there is the purely provincial aspect and, considering it, there does not seem to be any reason to make an investigation in that field.
With regard to the commutation or rather the decision not to commute the sentence, I am studying, in co-operation with the officials of my departments, what happened prior to the refusal to commute the sentence, and I hope to be able to make a statement in that regard before the adjournment of the house.

subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I wonder whether the minister can tell us if he has recently received any representations from the government of the province of Quebec, or anybody on its behalf, expressing its views in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, I did not hear the last part of the question. Expressing what?

subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: Expressing the views of the government of the province of Quebec in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I have received no representations from the government of Quebec.

subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: If the supplementary question is really urgent I will allow it, but I do not think even the original question was urgent.

subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: My supplementary question is, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: No doubt I should have specified in my answer-and I thought I did so- that besides having finished that reading, they are now considering what happened and what is contained in a bulky file, in connection with the statements contained in Mr. Hebert's book.

subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice related to his answers earlier in the day on the Coffin murder case, and in particular the suggested constitutional crisis between the then prime minister and the governor general. Did the minister investigate the alleged two day interval between the decision not to commute the sentence and the refusal or alleged refusal of the governor general to sign the necessary document?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: COFFIN CASE
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated the other day that I had communicated with the then prime minister, and I gave his report to the house. I was sorry that one newspaper report indicated that I had used the word "indignant" in respect of Mr. St. Laurent's conversation with me. That was not so. The reply I got from Mr. St. Laurent was not in the slightest degree one which denoted anything like that. He simply denied the report, and I am sure that as far as the house and the country are concerned that denial will have been accepted.
I might add that I did ask my officers to look at the records to ascertain if there had been any unusual delay in the matter. I find the facts to be as follows. The cabinet arrived at its decision on February 7, 1956. The order in council pertaining to the decision not to interfere with the sentence is dated February 8, 1956, and this decision was communicated to the provincial authorities early in the morning on February 9, 1956. The telegram from the sheriff confirming receipt of such advice was dispatched from Montreal at 10 a.m. on February 9, 1956. This contradicts and seems to dispose of the allegation that the governor general held the matter up for two days.

A moment ago, Mr. Speaker, when I answered a question directed to me by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette),

Inquiries of the Ministry existing legislation to prevent the sale of any corporation or the sale of any other property to anyone.

subtopic: SALE OF CANADIAN BANK SHARES TO FOREIGN PURCHASERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. In view of the reported intention of the Toronto-Dominion Bank to dispose of part of its assets to a foreign bank, and in view of the prohibition under section 99, subsection 2, of the Bank Act against such a transaction taking place without the minister's consent, can the minister tell us whether he is prepared to give consent to such a transaction if an application is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SALE OF CANADIAN BANK SHARES TO FOREIGN PURCHASERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been a certain amount of rumour that certain transactions of the Toronto-Dominion Bank might or might not be considered. The Toronto-Dominion Bank made an announcement at 11.15 this morning which perhaps hon. members have not seen. The announcement stated that the Toronto-Dominion Bank was making an investment in a bank to be known as the Midland and International Banks Limited, with head office in London, England, the other participants being the Midland Bank Limited, Standard Bank Limited of London, England and the Commercial Bank of Australia Limited. I do not know anything about any disposition of the assets of the Toronto-Dominion Bank. If there were any such contemplated, they would be dealt with in the ordinary course under the provisions of the law.

subtopic: SALE OF CANADIAN BANK SHARES TO FOREIGN PURCHASERS
speechtext:
I have a supplementary question on this matter which I believe should be directed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have not given him notice of this question. As the Minister of Finance said, a statement was issued by the Toronto-Dominion Bank at 11.15 this morning, with some preliminary rumours yesterday that some momentous statement was forthcoming; therefore I have not given notice to the minister of my intention to ask this question but he may take it as notice.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: SALE OF CANADIAN BANK SHARES TO FOREIGN PURCHASERS

As the hon. gentleman has said, I have not had an opportunity to think about this question. My offhand opinion would be

that there is room in this country for enlarged facilities for the financing of the export trade. I would hope that is the effect of this transaction.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre): Mr. Speaker, may I direct question to the Prime Minister. I am sorry he is not wearing the button that was given to him this morning. In view of the failure of the government and the delegation from Manitoba to reach a meeting of minds this morning with respect to the T.C.A. maintenance and overhaul base at Winnipeg, can the right hon. gentleman say what steps the government will now take to allay the dismay which all of us from Manitoba feel over this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: I do not feel there was a failure to reach a meeting of minds, and I do not think there is any cause for dismay with regard to the matter which the hon. member has mentioned.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister give an assurance that a public inquiry will be undertaken, as suggested by the premier of Manitoba, concerning the proposed reduction of employment in this overhaul and maintenance base in Winnipeg? I suggest this is something which the Prime Minister could do and ought to do in all the circumstances.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: The proposal which has been made will, we hope, lead to no reduction in employment but to the maintenance of employment, so the question was wrongly phrased in that respect. As far as an inquiry into the matter is concerned, I told the premier this morning I would discuss with him whether there should be such an inquiry, what the terms of reference of such an inquiry might be, and whether it should be held by the provincial or the federal government.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: I thank the Prime Minister for his general observations. May I ask, however, whether he will accept a public inquiry by the government of Canada jointly with the government of Manitoba to inquire into the peregrinations of this problem which have taken place since he took office.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: I have already stated I would discuss this matter with the premier of Manitoba, and the right hon. gentleman should surely realize that that is the proper way to proceed in a matter of joint interest of this kind.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext:
In
November the Prime Minister made a statement that employment in Winnipeg would not be reduced. In January the former minister said there would be a freeze of jobs. Close to 200 jobs had disappeared in Winnipeg. Can the government direct T.C.A. to maintain the freeze until a policy is worked out?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: As I have already said, it is the policy of the government to do everything possible to maintain employment at the T.C.A. base in Winnipeg and, if possible, to increase it.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister convey that desire of the government to Mr. McGregor, who is ignoring it?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: I would be very glad to do that, and also to convey to him the proceedings at the meeting this morning.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister aware that while this policy is in effect, employment at the base in Winnipeg is declining?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: I have asked for the figures with regard to employment in the base at Winnipeg, and for the figures of any decrease in T.C.A. employment in Winnipeg over the years. While there has been some decrease in recent months, there has also been a considerable increase in employment compared with ten years ago.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    EMPLOYMENT AT OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the Prime Minister's statement that there has been some progress in recent months, may I ask him to clarify this particular point. I put a written question on the order paper on November 13, which was answered. The question read as follows:
How many personnel have been transferred from the T.C.A. overhaul and maintenance base in Winnipeg to Montreal since April 22, 1963?
The answer given by the Minister of Transport was:
The management of Trans-Canada Air Lines advise as follows. During the period in question there have been five transfers, all of supervisory category, four of these at the individual's request and one at company request. No non-supervisory personnel have been transferred in the period.
In view of that answer, and in view of the statement made by the delegation this morning at the meeting which the Prime Minister attended that 170 people have been transferred in this interval, would it not be wise to have a public inquiry to get the facts of the case?

speechtext:
The information, Mr. Speaker, given to us this morning will be taken up with T.C.A. We will check the information
Inquiries of the Ministry against that which is available to T.C.A. and do our best to clear up this matter.

speechtext: I have a question for the Prime Minister. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of an interruption made last evening which I did not hear. That interruption came from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) and, as reported at page 5989 of Hansard, he said this:
I challenge the right hon. gentleman to show me where the word "nation" is in the English version of the present act and also to show me that we are deleting the word "national" from the present act.
I did not hear that question and that challenge last evening. It comes to me as somewhat of a surprise, in view of the fact that when he spoke on November 19, in explaining the reasons for the amendments to this act he said, as reported at page 4911 of Hansard:
Moreover, the word "national" in the English version is confusing in the context in which it is used, and resulted in another historical error in the French version. Thus, the latter constantly refers to the "centenary of the nation" rather than to the "centenary of confederation".
The expressions "Canada centennial", "centenaire du Canada", "national centennial" and "centenaire de la nation" have given rise to perfectly justified objections on the part of the premier of the province of Quebec.
He set down those objections in an exchange of correspondence first with the former prime minister of Canada and then with the present Prime Minister. That correspondence began on October 4, 1961, and has already been tabled in this house by the Minister of Justice, on June 27 of this year to be exact.
That correspondence and the debates which took place last summer in the legislative assembly show quite clearly that the government of Quebec will refuse to participate in the centennial celebrations, unless the changes we are proposing today are accepted by the Canadian parliament.

Now, sir, this challenge comes to me as rather a surprise, because I have before me the bill and it is apparent that the minister has not even read his own bill or the explanations therein. The challenge, I again point out, was to show the minister where they were deleting the word "national" from the present act. Therefore I commence by pointing out that clause 1 provides:
Section 1 of the National Centennial Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
In the explanatory notes it says:
The purpose of this amendment is to change the short title of the National Centennial Act.
Section 1 at present reads as follows: "1. This act may be cited as the National Centennial Act".
Clause 1 says:
"This act may be cited as the Centennial of Canadian Confederation Act".
So that "national" is removed twice there. Later on, in clause 2 it says:
Paragraph (a) of section 2 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(a) "Commission" means the centennial commission referred to in section 3;"
Then in the explanatory notes we find these words appear:
"Administration" means the national centennial administration referred to in section 3;"
Then it says in clause 3:
Section 3 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
At the moment section 3 reads:
There shall be a corporation to be called the national centennial administration-
That is now changed in this bill to the following:
There shall be a corporation to be called the centennial commission-
Then it sets out the members who shall comprise the commission. Finally, under clause 6 it say*:
Subsection (1) of section 10 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"10.	(1) There shall be a special account in
the consolidated revenue fund, to be known as the centennial of confederation fund, to which shall be credited the amounts appropriated by parliament for the purposes of the fund".
In the explanatory notes we find these words:
Subsection (1) at present reads as follows: "10. (1) There shall be a special account in the consolidated revenue fund, to be known as the national centennial fund, to which shall be credited the amounts appropriated by parliament for the purposes of the fund".
Therefore, sir, the challenge has been answered by simply indicating that the word "national" is removed in at least four or five cases throughout the act.

Now, Mr. Speaker, the minister is trying to squirm out of the position in which his smart question last evening placed him. In so far as that conference is concerned it says:
There shall be a national conference on the centennial of confederation-*
That is a different organization altogether. The hon. gentleman now, having made that loose statement last evening, finds himself in a situation where he tries to get out of the impossibility of the position in which he has placed himself by reason of an aimless interruption. While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, I ought to place on the record the letter from the premier of Quebec to the present Prime Minister. It is dated May 2, 1963:
Office of the Premier Province of Quebec
Hon. Lester B. Pearson,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ont.
My dear Prime Minister,
You no doubt know that the government of the province of Quebec has been invited to participate in the celebration of the centennial of confederation. This government has already expressed its intention of taking an appropriate part in that celebration by undertaking to pay its share of the cost of the memorial which is being erected in Charlottetown.
Unfortunately, a serious difficulty has made until now any kind of agreement impossible with the federal government.
As I pointed out in my letter of October 19, 1961 to the then prime minister of Canada-
And I interpolate here, that was ten days or so after the law had been passed by both houses.
-the act passed by the parliament of Canada is properly entitled an "act respecting the observance of the centennial of confederation in Canada", but that title is contradicted by section 3 and 17 which mention respectively the "national centennial" and "Canada's centennial".
Then he goes on to say:
It is obvious that it is not the title of the act that will catch the eye of the people, but
National Centennial Act
the names of the organizations set up to bring it into operation. ...We are therefore confident that you will admit the necessity of amending the act respecting the observance of the centennial of confederation in Canada in such a way as to eliminate the difficulties I have mentioned.
I draw attention to those excerpts from the letter as part of the answer to the challenge made last evening. I reiterate what I said then, that throughout the discussions, when the legislation was before the House of Commons, there was no objection raised by any of the members who sat opposite. Indeed, the present Prime Minister said on September 18, 1961:
The fact that we shall soon be celebrating our hundredth birthday makes us one of the older states in the world.
Then on another occasion, speaking in the house on the same date, he said, the reference being to myself:
As the Prime Minister has pointed out, it would be appropriate to examine the values of our national society.
In later speeches he said the same thing. For instance, speaking to the national federation of Liberal women-I emphasize the description of that organization; they have not had the feeling that "national" is a dangerous word-the right hon. gentleman said on October 29, 1963:
Canadians are going to grow together in national development, national purpose and national pride.
In all these cases "national" is used as it was used in the law passed by this parliament, the law which is now being amended. I simply wanted to clarify this and to point out that the hon. gentleman has not, apparently, read his own bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take a few minutes to try to calm down the few members who have just spoken about the matter under consideration.
At this time, when we in this house are thinking of celebrating confederation and attempts are being made to have us believe that we have succeeded in uniting the two great races into one nation, extremists have to take this occasion to try to push their extreme views one step further.
[Mr. Churchill.l

I think that the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) may have gone a little too far when he referred to the Queen, but if at this point an attempt is made to push this matter still further, to the extent of having someone state that this was right or that was wrong; if the word "national" is to become controversial with regard to confederation or centennial celebrations, then I wonder whether it would even be worth while to celebrate the centennial of confederation after all.
I admit that on some occasions, Quebec members have perhaps gone a little too far on the nationalist issue. This I recognize. But I would also ask the previous speakers to realize that on some occasions, other members have also carried their own brand of nationalism quite far.
I should also like to refer to the famous statement made by the previous speaker. Mr. Speaker, on a matter of such vital importance to the entire country, I wonder once again why petty politics has to be brought into this debate.
We earnestly wish to commemorate the centennial of confederation. We are anxious to show the world what a success this country has been. We want to show that it is possible for French speaking and English speaking Canadians to establish a true confederation. In that respect, I accept in good faith the explanation given by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) to the effect that Canada constitutes a political nation.
From the political point of view, we form a state, a country and a nation. I also agree with the minister when he states that from a cultural viewpoint, things are rather different, there being a French Canadian nation and an English Canadian nation.
Once again, I would ask hon. members of the opposition who spoke before me not to block this project which concerns all true Canadians who wish to celebrate a true confederation which has made it possible for two great races, two great nations, to establish so great and so fine a country as Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last few days, we have heard statements concerning the celebration of the centenary of confederation which were irresponsible in many respects.
Some members object and are deeply concerned because we are to celebrate the centenary of confederation instead of the centenary of the nation. As in the past, they have been trying to create a truly and fundamentally anti-Canadian climate.
On the other hand, others have said that there are two groups of extremists, one of

which is French Canadian, the other English Canadian, and both working against national unity in Canada.
I do not think that in this house there has been on our part, or on the part of French Canadian members, any hindrance or obstacle to understanding in this country. If there ever has been a conciliating nation or race these last 97 years, it should be recognized that it has been the population of the province of Quebec and French Canadian members.
Personally I do not agree with the opinion expressed the other day by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) to the effect that Canada recognizes the Queen of a foreign country. When we speak of Her Majesty the Queen, I see her as the Queen of Canada and not at all as the Queen of England. I think that Queen of Canada is her title as far as we are concerned.
We have to recognize more and more on the part of this sovereign, who is perfectly bilingual, that deep desire for unity, conciliation and understanding. Such an example might perhaps have been followed by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), who seems to have encountered many more difficulties than Her Majesty in the learning of French.
On the other hand, there are still people who talk about the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag and of a national anthem.
More and more, throughout the country, people have come to recognize the importance and urgency of adopting those measures or that measure that will provide Canada with a national distinctive flag and not a flag relating to a foreign emblem.
In this connection, I shall give as an example the small countries that have just recovered or obtained their freedom and independence. The first thing they did at this solemn moment in their history, was to adopt a distinctive national flag. Such was the case with Jamaica and African countries where, only a few days ago, that first step was taken once again.
When it has gained or is about to gain its sovereignty, the first action a country should take is to give itself a distinctive national flag and a national anthem.
For my part, in 1967, whether other people like it or not, if a flag bearing the union jack is presented as an English flag, I shall be the first to salute it to show my respect for the English, but should this flag be offered as the Canadian flag, well, there is a limit, and if it should come to that, I will not salute it, no matter what flag it is, unless it is Canada's own distinctive national flag.
This does not apply exclusively to the union jack. I would salute as well, with joy
National Centennial Act and veneration, the American flag which is the symbol of a friendly nation; but nobody could get me to believe that the American flag is our own national flag.
We are not faced with a problem of dissent, but with a problem of decision. If we recognize self-government and liberty for the smaller countries of the world, let us try at least to set an example, after several decades of existence as a dominion. I am sure that there is not a single representative, be he English or French speaking, who will object to the adoption of a national flag and a national anthem, which would be distinctly Canadian.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) stated yesterday afternoon that Canadians are showing their attachment to the idea of national unity in Canada. Let us remember, however, that national unity is not a one-way street. There cannot be exclusively rights for some and nothing but duties for others. We have on both sides, some rights and corresponding duties. Our main duty is precisely to try and understand each other the best we can.
I have said it, and I shall repeat it once more: I do not believe that an Englishman can be turned into a Frenchman, nor that a Frenchman can become an Englishman. However, I believe that it is possible to have two good Canadians, practising bonne entente and mutual understanding. In order to reach that goal, if it becomes necessary to water our wine, let us not hesitate. We have done just that and we ask our partners to do the same, so that we can sit at the same table, the table of confederation, of bonne entente, of understanding and co-operation. That is what we are asking for.
Yesterday, I was listening to the whining by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) concerning the use of the phrase "centennial of the nation" instead of "centennial of confederation" and he criticized the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) and asked the Prime Minister to give his opinion. If the right hon. gentleman keeps silent, it may be that he understands that it is up to parliament to decide. The Prime Minister alone does not decide. He introduces his legislation, but does not take the decision.
We should have liked to have his views. If he does not put them forward, at least some official representatives of the government have spoken. The Prime Minister and the Secretary of State made some statements yesterday. There were also statements made by the Conservatives. Only, as far as confederation is concerned, the Conservatives could have acted two or three years ago when they were sitting on your right, Mr. Speaker.

Now, if the government introduces such legislation, why lay the blame on the Prime Minister and ask him what he intends to do when the problem is settled. It does not belong to the Prime Minister to decide, but to parliament as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, I have nothing more to say for the time being, but I sincerely believe confederation, the centennial of confederation can be celebrated with enthusiasm in 1967, provided we are Canadians and not foreigners, provided we are bound to our Canadian country, and not to another country outside our frontiers, provided we play our part as Canadians and take our responsibilities in that respect, in order to reach the goal we are seeking, that is understanding, mutual co-operation and making Canada a greater country, where life is worth living.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is basically the same as in previous years being in accordance with the practice followed since 1952 and only differs in form in that it covers two calendar years instead of the usual one. As hon. members know, ordinarily there is a financing and guarantee bill presented to the house each year, but inasmuch as the 1962 legislation was not dealt with last year and the fiscal year 1963 is nearing completion it was deemed expedient to combine both years' authorizations and to present the bill at this time.
[Mr. Caouette.l

The 1962 capital budgets and 1961 annual reports of C.N.R. and T.C.A. were considered in November, 1962, by the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping, owned and controlled by the government. During the current session the 1963 capital budgets and 1962 annual reports of these crown corporations have been under consideration by a similar committee. The bill is intended to accomplish eight main purposes, each of which is similar in form to those of the 1961 act and preceding annual acts. These purposes are:
1.	To authorize capital expenditures by the Canadian National Railways not exceeding $156,500,000 during the 1962 calendar year as well as capital expenditures not exceeding $157 million during the 1963 calendar year.
2.	To authorize the company to make, prior to July 1, 1964, such capital expenditures as may be necessary to discharge obligations incurred under the 1962-63 act, but which become due for payment after January 1, 1964, as long as these expenditures do not exceed $56 million.
3.	To authorize the railway company to enter into contracts prior to July 1, 1964 for new equipment and for general additions and conversions, where payment will come due after the calendar year 1963, provided that such amounts do not exceed $31,200,000.
4.	To provide for the continued purchase by the Minister of Finance of Canadian National Railways 4 per cent preferred stock through to the end of the calendar year 1964. The 1961 financing and guarantee act extended to December 31, 1962, the expiry date of the authority granted by the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act, 1952, for the purchase of such stock up to the limit of 3 per cent of the company's gross revenue. In future years this provision might be among those affected if the government implemented the recommendations of the MacPherson commission and the proposals on the recapitalization of the C.N.R. While government decisions on these urgent and fundamental problems are pending, it is recommended that the bill extend the expiry date of this provision until the end of 1964.
5.	For the same reasons the bill also will extend until the end of 1964 the moratorium on interest on the government loan of $100 million to the railway company authorized by the capital revision act, 1952.
6.	The bill will contain a new section to increase to $480 million the limitation in the Canadian National Railways Refunding Act, 1955, placed on the authority to refund maturing or matured securities of the railway company. The limit is at present $230 million and it is necessary to increase this limit to allow the railway company to repay to the

government a loan of $250 million which the government advanced to the railway company for the purpose of refunding a bond issue in the same amount which matured on the 1st of February, 1963. The only foreseeable way that the C.N.R. could repay this government loan of $250 million would be to sell a bond issue of like amount to the public. There are no plans for such an issue. However, it is considered desirable to provide in this bill for such a possibility, should debt management considerations ever point in that direction.
7.	The bill will provide for the financing, either by means of the issue of new securities by the government of Canada or by way of direct loan, of an amount not to exceed $31,800,000. This amount represents the financial requirements of Trans-Canada Air Lines of $9,800,000 in the calendar year 1962, of $16 million in 1963 and $6 million during the first six months of 1964.
8.	Finally, as in previous years, the bill provides authority to make temporary loans to the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines to meet deficiencies in operating revenues up to June 30, 1964. As hon. members are aware, these loans to the two companies on income deficit account are of a temporary nature to meet deficiencies in revenue which regularly occur in the early part of each calendar year, and are repaid later either from annual revenues or, if these are insufficient, are written off by parliamentary appropriation.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to prolong this debate since I know that, as is the case usually, this legislation concerns particularly financial matters. However, as former minister of transport, I simply wish to take this opportunity to ask the government to study as soon as possible the advisability of allowing refinancing of the operations of the Canadian National Railways.
I believe it is already too long since we had a thorough study of the possibility of allowing the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways to adopt a new financing policy, in order that the company may not have to show each year an illogical deficit, which undermines the morale not only of the directors but also of all the employees of the Canadian National Railways.
That is why I have no objection whatsoever to the bill as it stands at the present time. I do not think it includes anything really new. However, when he appeared before the sessional committee, the president of the Canadian National Railways repeated
Canadian National Railways his arguments, which in fact are perfectly logical, in favour of a new capitalization policy for the Canadian National Railways.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will support this bill, but in doing so we would also raise the matter referred to by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), the long delay that seems to have been necessary, not just on the part of this government but the previous government, in making up their minds about the recapitalization program of Canadian National Railways. On the two most recent occasions the president of the railway has been before a house committee saying that the presentation has been made. On the third most recent occasion he was before us he gave us a long pep talk on all the advantages of recapitalization and what it would do for the railway. But despite all this long preparation we still have not had any action.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) suggests that it is up to the Department of Finance. I do not know what the Department of Finance thinks about it, but it might be as well if we had some explanation at this time. Since the bill really has an almost retroactive effect I would hope that the debate on it would not be long.
One weakness of the capital expenditures set-up of Canadian National Railways from our point of view has been that, with the argument for recapitalization, it is very difficult to know just how well the capital expenditures program for the last decade has worked. This is particularly true since Donald Gordon took over the management, and it is difficult to know how well this capital expenditure program has worked in putting the railway into what he now claims would be an efficient position, as a matter of fact a position without deficit in 1963, if the Mac-Pherson recommendations on recapitalization had been carried out. This claim of Mr. Gordon's is one that is difficult to understand or appreciate. It is easier to see when you look at the long term debt of Canadian National Railways and the fantastic interest payments which have to be made.
I suppose our Social Credit friends would have a solution for the most disturbing point, one which would be more apparent and easier than any that I could offer. However, I tend to go along with their line of reasoning on this. Over the last six or seven years Canadian National Railways have had too many debenture or bond issues floated at rates of interest of 5 per cent or more. This may have been necessary in order to meet the market of the time, but one wonders, when

Canadian National Railways the government of Canada has such borrowing powers, whether this tremendous increase in the percentage of interest on the C.N.R. debt for these more recent capital expenditures is not too high. I would hate to think that in another ten years, if recapitalization does go through, another president of Canadian National Railways will be coming along to have the debt shifted again on to the back of the government of Canada, because of the high interest rates that were charged on Canadian National borrowings during the fifties and sixties. It is for this reason I think we would appreciate a statement from the Department of Finance as to its attitude towards recapitalization of the whole Canadian National debt structure.
In the meantime, this is a routine measure and only touches that other matter by implication. We have, therefore, nothing further to say.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking the floor simply to say that we do not refuse in the least to support this bill since it is only legalizing expenditures incurred last year and this year. I think we would be playing a dirty trick on the C.N.R. and all other agencies related to it if we refused to support this bill.
However, it enables us to notice the financial situation in which the C.N.R. finds itself and to show to everyone-even to those who refuse to believe in the Social Credit theories -that those debts that keep piling up are incurred just to reimburse loans made previously.
If the people are happy with this system, they can keep it; but if they are not satisfied with it, nor with Social Credit, they should by all means find quickly a system that will rid us of those chronic debts which only increase year after year.
I would also like to say a word on the management of Canadian National Railways which, judging by what we hear, is most adequate. We are ready to recognize this, inasmuch as the directors will prove it to us but, as a matter of fact, this bill involves, besides Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines and it is difficult to examine its budgets and balance sheets, since they are included with those of Canadian National Railways, whose directors are unwilling to reveal the amounts involved, claiming that this is an altogether different company.
I think the government should hereafter consider separating these two crown corporations. Because these are public companies; hon. members, who are the representatives
IMr. Fisher.l
of the people, must be made aware, on behalf of the people, of all expenditures and; they must know what constitutes the income and what the resulting balance is.
I admit, as the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) said a while ago, that we now have a sham deficit, if we consider the operations for this year. Nevertheless, we are in a situation of chronic indebtedness which will prevent the C.N.R. and T.C.A. from making profits, because our economic system is no more adequate this year than last.
To conclude, I should like to make a short comment on the hotels operated by the C.N.R. Because the Social Credit party claims to be the party of free or private enterprise, its opponents tell us that private companies make exorbitant profits and are hurtful to some other concerns.
I have seen the operation reports of the C.N.R. hotels and I understand that only the Queen Elizabeth hotel, which is run by a private company, made profits, but so much so that it succeeded in erasing the deficits of all other C.N.R. hotels.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this is food for thought. This is not a matter of demagogy, but only of recording facts and figures. If other hon. members can offer better solutions, they should better do it fast, since we are sinking into conditions which worsen year after year, and even if we still exist in 1967 to celebrate the centennial of confederation, we will find ourselves in a financial situation which will prevent us from doing so.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity we have of studying Bill No. C-127 to
speak on a subject which made the headlines in papers all over the country, namely the decision of the president of T.C.A. in favour of the American DC-9.
I will try to be brief. I was reading in the Saturday, November 5, 1963 issue of Le Devoir a statement of principle, a testimony of faith by the Liberal members from the province of Quebec. The newspaper report is as follows:
The Liberal members from Quebec will recommend to the federal government the purchase of the Caravelle jetliners.
Ottawa-It is the intention of the Liberal members from the province of Quebec to recommend to the federal government the purchase of the French jet Caravelle instead of the American DC-9 in order to alleviate the tragic situation which prevails at the Canadair plant of Ville Saint Laurent, near Montreal.
Under the chairmanship of Mr. Guy Rouleau, M.P. for Dollard, the Quebec Liberals have decided to form a study and working committee which will make recommendations to the government in that respect.
According to them, there is serious unemployment at present in northern Montreal and especially

In Ville Saint Laurent, because Canadair has no contracts. The company has kept only 3,187 of Its 6,500 regular employees.
Liberal members from Quebec see only one solution to the problem, that is the purchase by T.C.A. of the Caravelle jetliner which would be built by Canadair.
Therefore, it will be the committee's mission to convince the federal government and especially the Department of Transport to choose the Caravelle instead of the American DC-9 which would be partly built in the Toronto area but which would be assembled in the United States.
The French company, Sud-Aviation, promised to conclude an agreement with Canadair for the construction of the Caravelle, if Trans-Canada Air Lines decided to buy a sufficient number of those jets.
The government of Quebec, the city of Montreal and Ville Saint Laurent have already submitted representations in that respect.
Local 712 of the international association of machinists has also submitted urgent recommendations to the hon. member for Dollard.
The committee is made up of Mr. Rouleau, the chairman, and of Messrs. Raymond Rock (Jacques Cartier-Lasalle), Pit Lessard (St. Henry), Gerard Loiselle (St. Ann), Prosper Boulanger (Mer-cier), Vincent Drouin (Argenteuil-Deux-Monta-gnes) and Jean Rochon (Laval).
Mr. Speaker, I was anxious to read to the house this press report published in nearly all our Canadian newspapers, because it is an ultimatum by the federal representatives from Quebec, to force the government to choose the Caravelle, so as to cope with the unemployment which besets Quebec, and more particularly the island of Montreal, which includes the town of Saint Laurent.
I was astonished to see that the pressures exercised by the representatives have come to nothing, and that when the Prime Minister told the house about the choice of the DC-9, the same members on the treasury benches, (all of them from Quebec), thunderously applauded.
Mr. Speaker, after that statement which, as I said, is really an ultimatum, I am amazed by the actions of the representatives who sit on the treasury benches and who signed the petition.
Mr. Speaker, pressures, supported by countless documents, had also been exerted by the authorities of the province of Quebec, by Mr. Lapalme and by Mr. Rene Levesque. The following account was given as to it:
Let us remember that Mr. Rene Levesque, who is the minister of natural resources in the Lesage cabinet, stated as early as October last: "The Quebec government will have recourse to all firm and friendly means of exerting pressure to endeavour to persuade federal authorities of the necessity to pick out the Sud-Aviation Caravelle aircraft, to modernize Trans-Canada's air fleet-
And Mr. Rene Levesque had this to add:
-that he had attracted criticisms from Ottawa for having stated that the Quebec government was exerting "polite but persistent" pressures so as to guide the company's choice, has disclosed yesterday that the cabinet possesses "well supported" files regarding the respective worthiness
Canadian National Railways of the aircraft among which Trans-Canada Air Lines must make their choice and that the superiority of the Caravelle aircraft is undoubtedly unquestionable,
As I have said, Mr. Lapalme made those statements, supported by labour representatives in Canada and, especially in the province of Quebec.
However, Mr. Speaker, we were surprised by T.C.A.'s decision, concerning the choice of the DC-9 aircraft, which was approved afterwards by the government, and we were particularly surprised by the statement made by Mr. McGregor, president of this crown corporation whose salary is paid by the Canadian taxpayers. In my opinion, he should have been more careful in his statements and he should not have tried to foster trouble and stir up strife. The president of T.C.A. made unfortunate statements. I would refer to what Mr. Therrien, a member of the Glassco commission, said again recently:
It is not the ill-timed statements of a man like Mr. McGregor, president of T.C.A., who, more than anybody else, should refrain from evaluating the qualifications of the French Canadians in administration. No such statements can help settle the problem to the satisfaction of the French-Canadian nation.
Mr. McGregor even stated that it was quite possible that T.C.A. would remain unilingual, as it would be too expensive, and thousands of dollars would have to be spent to have the words "Air Canada" inscribed on the corporation's aircraft. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether intensification of bilingualism in this country should be measured by the amount of dollars likely to be involved.
However, Mr. Speaker, as I have said, it would have been so important to award T.C.A. that contract, to Canadair providing work for thousands of Canadian workers and their families for five years.
It should not be forgotten that Sud-Aviation would have built all the Caravelle aircraft here, whereas only certain parts of the DC-9 will be built here, while other parts will be built in the United States. The bulk of the work will be done in the United States. That was the opinion of a Montreal newspaper quoted earlier; and this statement was signed by many members from Quebec.
There is also something else, Mr. Speaker. The DC-9 still has to be tested. Moreover, American firms are being encouraged to build these aircraft themselves and in fact, most parts will be built in the United States, and this at a moment when we have a deficit with that country.
Mr. McGregor even questioned the efficiency of the Caravelle. In my opinion, he showed a lack of judgment and contributed to intensify the tension between France and Canada, at a time when our Prime Minister

Canadian National Railways is going to visit France in a few weeks. I think that was a poor thing to say when one considers that the Caravelle has carried 7 million passengers over 60 million miles, which is equal to 2,500 times around the earth and 130 times the distance to the moon. Moreover, the Caravelle is used not only in France, but by 23 companies throughout the world.
Another statement made before the committee and which surprised me was when Mr. McGregor attempted to question the competence of French speaking Canadians.
I think he should first do like the president of another crown corporation, that is try to find at least one or two French speaking persons to appoint to the board of directors, consisting of nine members.
Furthermore, McGregor added that the Caravelle was an excellent aircraft eight years ago but that it is outdated today. I am quite surprised that the president of this crown corporation does not know that the Caravelle Super B which will be in operation in 1964, is a much better aircraft than the Caravelle now in use.
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted in closing to give to the house statistics taken from the British magazine Flight International.
The following figures represent the activities of the different models of aircraft in the world and the number of accidents they have had. These figures are applicable up to the month of May 1963. They indicate, for instance, that the Boeing 707 with 210 aircraft in service, has had 32 accidents, 9 being fatal, since it has been put into operation. With 60 aircraft in operation, the Comet has had 16 accidents, 5 being fatal; the DC-8, 185 in operation, 15 accidents, 7 being fatal; the Boeing 720, 129 in operation, 11 accidents, 2 being fatal; the Caravelle, 151 in operation, 7 accidents, 4 being fatal; the Convair 800, no figures as to number in operation or number of accidents, but this aircraft has had one fatal accident.
And to complete this list, since May 30, 1963, the Caravelle has had one fatal accident. The BAC-111 has had one fatal accident and the DC-8 has had two accidents, one of them fatal, that is the recent accident at Ste. Therese de Blainville.
In the light of the statements made by the president of T.C.A. which have gone a long way to damage our national unity as well as the relations between France and Canada, I wonder whether the government could not compel this crown corporation to publish the report of its experts on the choice of the DC-9, in order to shed some light on the matter for the benefit of the public?


Besides, part of that report relating to the maintenance and repair base in Winnipeg was made known to the government of Manitoba.
I also wonder whether the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) or the government should not oblige Mr. McGregor to mend his ways, so as to put right not only the damage he brought to our national unity, but also the deterioration of our relations with a friendly country like France.
Mr. Speaker, those are the few remarks I wished to make.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks shall be brief. We are presented

with a bill for the year 1962-63 and also for new investments covering a period ending in July 1964.
I think it is important to mention here that the C.N.R., a crown corporation, shows a deficit every year, which entails an increase in its debt and new bond issues at quite high rates of interest, especially when you consider that only one or two issues carried interest at the rate of 5 per cent in the last ten years, while all others were over 5| per cent and even 6 per cent in some cases.
While these deficits accrue from year to year, we are told that a substantial proportion of the new investments will be to help T.C.A. meet its obligations, expand and buy new aircraft, which represents quite a large amount.
But, as was indicated by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) at a meeting of the railways committee, a balance sheet of T.C.A. is not presented to us under the pretext that it is a completely different corporation from the C.N.R.
I note that the former minister of transport made a very brief statement on this bill, but when you realize that T.C.A. operates a transportation system in some parts of Canada in direct competition with companies which have invested large amounts of money in the last three or five years to improve their service and make it adequate to meet today's needs, you start wondering. And on that score, I could refer to the case of Quebecair which has made very large capital investments in the last three years following the promise that T.C.A. would give up the service between Quebec and Montreal and on the north shore, where service is also provided by Quebecair. Besides, it has been established that T.C.A. operates at a loss between Quebec and the north shore, and Quebecair has to compete now with a crown corporation.
The same thing exists in the trucking field. There were statements made by C.N.R. representatives to the effect that this year again they would continue to compete with private companies already existing through their road transportation system. It is the same thing again with the hotel business where, among others, the Queen Elizabeth hotel, owned by the C.N.R., shows a profit, and it is operated in direct competition with private enterprise. In short, that crown corporation branches out in three important directions, truck transport, air transport and hotel business.
Today, with this bill, we are called upon to vote rather substantial amounts in order to facilitate the refinancing of balance sheets in continuous deficit. Who will pay these amounts? It is always the Canadian taxpayer who pays the cost.
Canadian National Railways
It seems to me, as mentioned by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) that some suggestions might be in order; therefore, may I offer you my own suggestion. A complete study of the refinancing of all the assets now administered by the C.N.R. should be undertaken as soon as possible to consider the advisability of financing that crown corporation in new ways less costly and, in the last analysis, cheaper for the Canadian people, so that we may have truly well organized services without having to submit measures that cost a lot of money to the country.
In short, we are seeing competition between crown corporations and private enterprise which has invested huge sums of money. We should give greater protection to private trucking companies, especially from organizations like the C.N.R. which asks us each year for rather large amounts when already adequate services are financed by private enterprise.
In my opinion, we should look for a new method of refinancing in full the C.N.R.

It was explained to us by the president of the company that six factors were applied in the choice of an aircraft. I believe five of them were under consideration. The airplanes were rated according to the six factors, and the airplane which had the highest rating-that is, which served T.C.A.'s interests best-was the one they chose.

The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) says there is no doubt the Caravelle is the best aircraft. I submit there is a great deal of doubt. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was quite pleased a moment ago to hear the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) who is perfectly familiar with the situation of Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines recommend a refinancing of the debt with a view to reducing the interest on it.
Well, we notice that the ideas advocated by our group in this house are beginning to find their way into the minds and this is a good thing. I know some of our good Liberal friends would be quite pleased to have certain monetary reforms carried out, when they find it impossible to administer the country according to their wishes and views.
Our ideas about the monetary reform are becoming increasingly essential to the administration of this country. Every day we find new evidence of this, especially with the study of the bill now before us, which reveals this enormous debt, impossible to pay, but that will have to be cleared some day, because we cannot continue, under such a system, to maintain so considerable a debt.
A while ago I heard the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) say: Of course I do not advocate the easy solutions of the Social Credit, but I favour a decrease and a refinancing of the debt of C.N.R.
So let me ask this question: Is it more difficult to create credit as a debt than to create credit without debts? Is the operation not exactly the same?
Now, I say that to write down figures in a book indicating an issue of credit at a 6 per cent rate of interest or an issue of credit at 1 per cent is the same kind of operation. In fact, what difference is there really in the writing down of figures and what technical problems can there be?
It seems to me that one does not have to be extremely bright to understand that.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I will say this: The Canadian National Railways will never be able to make any profits so long as they face a debt of that kind. This is one of the most important questions the government should examine in order to solve this extremely serious problem which, in my opinion, cripples much of Canada's economy.

Just one word, Mr. Speaker, concerning paragraph 2 of clause 3 of the measure now before us; it says this:
(2) The national company, with the approval of the governor in council, is authorized
(a)	at any time prior to the 1st day of July, 1964, to borrow money by the issue and sale of securities or by way of loan from the Minister of Finance to provide the amounts required by Trans-Canada Air Lines for the purposes mentioned in paragraphs (a) and (b) of subsection (1); and

Mr. Speaker, under clause 3, the Canadian National Railways is authorized to make capital expenditures amounting to $157 million and those expenditures	are	distributed as

Road property	$114,134,000
Branch line construction	4,166,000
Hotels	3,797,000

Mr. Speaker, I shoud like to point out that, this year, $3,797,000 are allocated to hotels compared to $1,480,000 last year.
Mr. Speaker, under paragraph (2) of clause 3, the Canadian National Railways is authorized to borrow money by the issue and sale of securities. But if a crown corporation has had deficits for many years, where will it take those securities to be issued? Where will it go and from whom will it borrow those amounts? In short, to whom will it sell those securities it will decide to market?
Mr. Speaker, the same paragraph stipulates also:
-by the issue and sale of securities or by way of loan from the Minister of Finance-
Now, how will the Minister of Finance be able to finance the sum of $157 million required by the Canadian National Railways?
And at this point let me say incidentally that Trans-Canada Air Lines also shows a deficit each year.
Where will the Minister of Finance get the money to make a loan to the C.N.R.?
Mr. Speaker, reference was made a while ago to the fact that T.C.A. and the C.N.R., and especially the latter, often used those amounts to compete unfairly with private enterprise.
An hon. member mentioned earlier that in the hotel trade, only the hotels run by private enterprise were making profits. And yet, the government presists in competing with private enterprise in other fields.
The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron) pointed out to the house that the trucking industry was subject to fierce competition from the C.N.R. I do not think it is in the

Canadian National Railways best interests of Canada that crown corporations, including the C.N.R., should thus compete with private enterprise.
On the one hand, private enterprise is being taxed in order to finance the deficits of crown corporations, indirect taxes are levied, etc. In the provincial field, the trucking business must pay very high charges for truck licence plates, etc. And, with all those expenditures, it is almost a miracle that the trucking business can remain in operation throughout Canada and in every province.
Now, as the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote) rightly pointed out just now, if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), in order to finance the operations of crown corporations, were to borrow from the Bank of Canada at a nominal interest rate not exceeding administrative costs, he would not have to pay the same deficit two or three times, or two or three times the cost of building a railway line, and even twice the amount for repairs, because capital bears interest, that is, the interest reaches the same amount as the capital created at the beginning.
From a mathematical point of view, it is impossible to repay twice the amount of the loan.
Mr. Speaker, we suggest that the goven-ment should use the Bank of Canada, and not only to finance the C.N.R., but in all fields.
Mr. Speaker, we have said many times, and rightly so, that it would be cheaper to resort to debt-free money than to debt-tied money which requires that such amount be greater in the end than when it was first created.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that even if the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) does not understand all the principles or theories of the Social Credit, it is obvious that the Minister of Finance could at least try the experiment once, to realize to what extent it could help the Canadian people as a whole. Instead of levying taxes that grow higher each year, we could consider a possible reduction of taxes, precisely because we would create the equivalent for crown corporations or the administration of public affairs in all fields, educational, municipal, provincial and federal.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that in a few years from now the government would be happy to be able to lighten the tax burden which now weighs heavily on the shoulders of the Canadian taxpayer.
Before resuming my seat, I would not forgive myself if I did not point out how important it is, for the parliament of Canada, to help private enterprise, as much as possible, because it has not failed in Canada.
