maintopic: GOOD NEWS BROADCASTING ASSOCIATION OF CANADA

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, December 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-15, to incorporate the Good News Broadcasting Association of Canada-Mr. Enns-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GOOD NEWS BROADCASTING ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to take the time of the committee for a few minutes to put on the record, certainly the views of this member and I think of a number of other members who constituted the committee which considered this bill in the miscellaneous private bills committee, and the reasons, apart altogether from the individuals involved in this particular case, why I think it would not be in the best public interest to enact this kind of legislation.
We discovered during the course of the rather prolonged hearings in the committee that this particular organization was one which arose out of a movement that had originated in the state of Nebraska, and which had ultimately achieved incorporation itself within the state of Nebraska. Subsequently the movement decided to undertake a Canadian operation and obtained a licence from the province of Manitoba, or rather, the Nebraska corporation obtained a licence from Manitoba to carry on its activities within that province. Subsequently the Nebraska corporation extended its activities throughout Canada, and I think the activities are adequately stated in the explanatory notes and in the powers of the bill. They basically involved the broadcasting of evangelical messages throughout Canada.
I would like to make it perfectly clear, and I am sure this feeling is shared by the other members on the committee, that we have no objection whatsoever to that type of broadcasting. We certainly have no criticism at all of the reverend gentleman who is responsible for the development of this particular organization in Nebraska. Indeed, viewing the financial statements of the Nebraska organization, and viewing the fact that he has in a period of approximately 15 years attained for that corporation total assets in excess of $1 million, one can only admire both his sincerity and his faith, and point out that the organization which he has built up to the present and the very broad activities which it carries out, is a tribute to his own personal character.
28902-5-382i
Private Bills
However, I would like to point out that in enacting this bill we would be creating not only a precedent, which might be taken advantage of by subsequent applicants for incorporations by way of private bills in this house, but we may also be creating a corporate body which, when the reverend gentleman to whom I have made reference, in due course passes on, might fall into the hands of a much less scrupulous and a much less devoted group of successors.
What the bill proposes to do is to create, by way of a private act, a corporation with no distinct congregation or body of members which will be able to control the directors or trustees, as they are referred to in this particular bill. In other words, a group of trustees or directors are being set up who are beyond the control of any particular group of supporting members. They will be entitled to carry on the corporation's activities, they will be entitled to solicit a very large amount of funds across Canada, and will be entitled to spend those funds and apply them for such purposes as they wish, without ultimately presenting their accounting to the control of any particular congregation.
Hon. members will at once see there is a sharp distinction here between the type of corporation proposed in this bill and the type of corporation such as the Lutheran corporation which we considered earlier today. In that case there is a congregation; there is a situation where you have a defined body of members who ultimately reserve the rights, and have property rights reserved under the law for the purpose of controlling that particular ministry.
There is no defined body of members in the Good News Broadcasting Association of Canada who will be in the position of controlling the board of trustees and controlling the ministry. Therefore the consequence is that there is no one basically to whom an accounting is to be made. There is no one to control the trustees in the course of their solicitation for public funds. There is no one ultimately to control the manner in which the funds are to be spent, the extent to which these funds shall be spent on expenses and the charitable purposes for which they are to be devoted, and in general terms to make certain the trustees in this particular case stick within the framework of their particular powers.
It is known that the corporate power conferred by this parliament can be withdrawn by this parliament, but I suggest in practical terms it will not be easy, or in fact practical, for any particular individual who may question the manner in which the corporation has been carried on, to come back to parliament, and obtain a repeal of the statute.

Private Bills
I would point out that the problem involved in religious or charitable bodies of this kind has been met at various levels, and some of the provinces have various provisions, such as the province of Ontario, which has enacted a statute known as the charities accounting act. This act sets down a defined procedure whereby a body soliciting and applying for funds in the province must make an accounting to the public trustee of the province, a civil servant, an emanation of the government. They must make an accounting to the public trustee, as I say; they must explain how the funds have been applied, and when funds have been solicited or received they must make periodic returns of the amounts received and the persons from whom they were received. What is equally important are the provisions under section 6 of the Ontario charities accounting act whereby, to quote subsection 1:
Any person may complain as to the manner In which a person or organization has solicited or procured funds by way of contribution or gift from the public for any purpose, or as to the manner in which any such funds have been dealt with or disposed of.
May I point out, Mr. Chairman, that machinery of that kind, and control provisions such as those contained in the charities accounting act of Ontario, are not paralleled at the federal level. There is no machinery such as is provided for by this Ontario statute which would enable individuals who are critical of the manner in which funds have been solicited or spent by a charitable organization to obtain any public review by any government body with regard to those particular activities.
I also point out that there is a very real question of doubt as to whether or not a provincial statute such as the one I have referred to would apply to a company incorporated under a private act of this parliament. Indeed, in the course of the committee hearings I expressly questioned the solicitor for the association as to whether or not the body, which is now authorized to do business in Manitoba and in fact is engaging in business throughout Canada, has raised funds in Ontario. He said yes, and he also acknowledged the fact that he made no returns under the Ontario law; and what is more, he said he did not have any intention of making returns under that law. He took the position that the provincial acts did not apply. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, there is a real doubt as to whether these provincial provisions can apply. Therefore, not only is federal machinery missing, but it is fairly clear also that the provincial machinery will be inapplicable.
It was suggested in the course of the committee's hearings that the various taxing au-
[Mr. Macdonald.1
thorities, who from time to time have the duty of conferring upon these bodies charitable status to entitle them to the tax deductions and exemptions available to charities, would in some way exercise some kind of police influence over the body in question. Without questioning the fact that the revenue will from time to time devote close consideration as to the amount spent by such a body or as to the manner in which it otherwise employs its funds, I suggest that the apparatus of the Department of National Revenue is, first, not available to question the manner in which funds are raised; and second, it is only partly available to look into the manner in which the funds are applied. Taxing authorities such as the Department of National Revenue may very well be interested in the amount of expenses, but there is no provision available for an individual to take exception to the manner in which the funds have been expended and to require some kind of accounting of the manner in which the funds have been used. He cannot require this through the taxing statutes.
It was also pointed out during the course of the hearings that there was a full audit of the operations of this particular corporation in Canada. I would point out, as I pointed out at that time, that no doubt it is true that an audit provides interested persons with a better understanding of the financial position of such a corporation, but an audit provides no kind of assurance at all as to the manner in which the funds may have been applied. An audit will tell us how much quantitatively was spent in what direction, but it has no way of qualitatively assessing the manner in which the particular funds were expended by the board of trustees.
Therefore I would submit, Mr. Chairman, that we would be creating a corporate body here which is in the position of soliciting large amounts of funds-and experience indicates they have had success in soliciting large amounts of funds-from people throughout Canada, and that the body will be substantially beyond the jurisdiction of any controlling authority in Canada, including the jurisdiction of the people who may actually provide the funds. There is nothing in this bill, as there is so often in the case of charitable institutions, under part II of the Companies Act of Canada, saying that a contributor of a certain amount shall become a sustaining member, that the contributor of a further amount shall become an honourary life member, and so on. There is no provision, in fact, decreeing who a member shall be, or that by reason of their financial contribution they shall be entitled to a particular right, such as to question the activities of the corporation.

I think it would be an unsound principle for this legislature to adopt the practice of creating such corporate bodies. It is for this reason that I personally expressed my opposition to this measure when it was before the committee. In doing so, Mr. Chairman, let me just reaffirm that I respect the good faith of the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa in bringing this matter before the house. I also respect the good faith, as I say, of the reverend gentleman who sought this incorporation and who has had such success in his evangelic methods. But I do not think this house should engage in the creating of such a corporate body, which substantially will not be responsible to the people from whom it receives its funds.

maintopic: GOOD NEWS BROADCASTING ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say only a few words about this bill. I think that because it has been passed through the committee and is back in the house we should today express the opinion of the committee of the whole and of the house, if there is a difference of opinion, and come to a conclusion on this bill. I know that in the miscellaneous private bills committee the decision was finally made to report the bill with certain amendments, which are before us. I acknowledge that those who are opposed to the bill are opposed to it by virtue of honest belief that there is not sufficient control in connection with this company which seeks incorporation.
I would just like to make two comments, Mr. Chairman. First, I think this is a basic case of religious freedom. Second, we discussed in committee ways in which any improper action by the broadcasting company could be avoided. We brought in amendments in fairly large quantity which legally, I think would encompass the corporation with a great many limitations that were not originally intended. So I think there is no possibility of the corporation carrying on a business for which there is no supervision.
I want to comment on one of the remarks of the hon. member for Rosedale in this regard.
In the committee there was no suggestion whatever of impropriety. This is a company which is making "Back to the Bible" broadcasts to the people, mainly in western Canada but also elsewhere in this country. There was never any question that the broadcasts were improper or were doing anything except providing the straight dissemination of the religious viewpoint of the Bible as seen by Reverend Epps, who appeared before the committee. There was no suggestion that Reverend Epps was not a straightforward and honest broadcaster whose messages are listened to in many remote sections of Canada where people have no opportunity of going to church. There is no suggestion at all that
Private Bills
there is anything improper about these broadcasts. There were suggestions that perhaps the whole set-up was not tight enough to prevent abuses of the privilege that parliament was being asked to grant with regard to charitable donations.
One of the clauses in the bill states that the object of the corporation, among others, is to accept charitable donation. Some members of the committee feared that the inclusion of this object in the bill might give the broadcasting corporation automatic status as a charitable organization in the light of which they could say to those responsible for collecting income tax: We do not need to qualify as a charitable organization because we have been qualified by parliament. To prevent such a thing happening an amendment was introduced to subclause (c) of clause 4 stating that this provision would not relieve the corporation of the necessity of complying with the provisions of any other statute relating to charitable organizations.
Thus, this organization is still required to make returns to the income tax department in order to qualify as a charitable organization. I make this appeal to the committee. This is a progressive corporation with religious objects. No impropriety was ever suggested with regard to it. If we deny the request of this organization we shall be denying it equality before the law in the parliament of Canada. Other organizations are incorporated to carry out religious and charitable objectives and the same privilege should be extended to this organization, regardless of the fact that it has its origins in the United States. For these reasons I appeal to the committee to let this matter come to a vote and, when the vote is reached, to support this bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GOOD NEWS BROADCASTING ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to ask him a question? Would he not agree that it would be desirable in the case of this religious body, as in the case of all others which come before the house, that there should be some ultimate control exercisable by those who give their financial support over the manner in which the ministry is conducted?

maintopic: GOOD NEWS BROADCASTING ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
The question is a reasonable one. It was raised in the committee. There are directors, all of whom must be Canadians, as provided in this particular bill. There is no church congregation in the ordinary sense of that word. It would be impossible to have one in the circumstances in which this organization is set up. The corporation broadcasts its appeals. It receives contributions, presumably in small sums of money-one dollar, or two dollars. People put these sums in envelopes and send them

Private Bills
in to support the broadcasts and the missionary work. But by the very nature of the operation there is not a congregation in the normal sense of that word.
The operation must, therefore, be carried on by those who have banded together to run it. There are seven or nine general directors of the world wide organization, and there are three in Canada. I admit there is not a congregation in the normal sense; neither are we establishing a religion or a church. We are merely recognizing a state which exists; we are recognizing an organization which makes broadcasts and which requests funds. I point out again that in this bill, and particularly in the terms of the amendment, we have required this organization to make a return under the Companies Act and under the Income Tax Act. These conditions have been tightened up as far as possible, and although there is no congregation there is a governing body which is responsible to the organizations to which reports are made. There is no provision for an annual meeting. It would virtually be impossible to bring together all the people who have made contributions so as to hold such a meeting. It would be too much to expect those who had contributed a dollar, or two dollars, or even ten dollars, to travel the length and breadth of this country in order to take part in an annual meeting.
I think we have to recognize the existence of this organization. To say it is different is not to say we should not allow it to operate. I do not think we have a right to tell a religious organization how it should operate. I do not think we have the right to say who shall be the officials of such an organization or how it shall be set up. If we did that, we should be getting into trouble. I think we must recognize that this is a religious body, that it is set up in the best way open to us, and that we have to accept it.

maintopic: GOOD NEWS BROADCASTING ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
There are one or two questions I should like to direct to the sponsor of this bill. I may say that from what I know of the Good News Broadcasting Corporation I agree with the remarks which have been made; it in sincere in its attempt to promote Christianity. I would not disagree with that. But I was not a member of the committee and I should like to know whether donations to this organization qualify at the present time for exemption from income tax, particularly in Manitoba. I should like also to know whether this body has encountered any resistance from provincial governments or other groups with regard to its activities in the provinces. I agree that an amendment such as has been described might answer many of the doubts some members have felt, but even

though the technicalities of the law may have been met I believe we must be concerned to see that funds are dispersed in accordance with the wishes of those who contribute. It would be interesting to know whether, if this act were passed, the organization would have the authority from parliament to circumvent provincial statutes set up to control charitable organizations.

maintopic: GOOD NEWS BROADCASTING ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext: I would like to ask the sponsor of the bill to answer those questions.

maintopic: GOOD NEWS BROADCASTING ASSOCIATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
First of all, the hon. member asked whether contributions to this organization are deductible under the Income Tax Act. The answer is, yes. For a number of years the corporation has had the authority to issue receipts which are acceptable as showing that certain sums have been donated to a charitable organization.
The hon. member asked if there had been any objection from the provinces or provincial bodies with regard to the activities of this corporation across Canada. I would say there have been no registered official objections as far as any provincial government or organization is concerned. There has been no organized objection to this group per se. The very fact that it is expanding its services is testimony to the value these programs must have to the many citizens who listen to them. Donations are voluntary. No one knocks on any door. People want to listen to the programs or they do not. They can turn their radios off if they wish. Few church organizations can exist on the basis of so loose a financial structure. Many churches live on pledges. This is done entirely by voluntary support. Testimony was given before the committee that over one million letters had been received in the past year alone. This is good testimony to the usefulness of, or to the need for, an operation of this kind.
I believe the next question which the hon. member asked related to the availability of an auditor's statement, or of a financial statement. I think the undertaking is certainly present that any donor requesting a financial statement can have his request granted.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) has already mentioned how difficult it would be to conduct annual meetings when there are listeners from British Columbia to Newfoundland. This is entirely a national organization. You cannot very well bring people in to these meetings; you could not have a big enough hall to hold all the people who are interested. Therefore it is left to those persons desirous of getting a factual statement to see that this will be provided. I merely want to reiterate that the service of

the Good News Broadcasting Corporation is widely endorsed across Canada, just as it is in the United States.
There was some objection raised about this company having a parent organization in the United States. I do not think this objection is relevant because religion is not a national item and we really would not want to object on that ground, I am sure. The fact that the organization has come to the parliament of Canada for incorporation means, by that very act alone, that it is accepting further imposition or restriction. Because whether or not parliament passes the bill the company will continue operating, and there is really nothing which can be done to stop them. What they are doing now is becoming a Canadian corporation and subjecting themselves to the further regulation that this implies. I appeal to all hon. members of the house to give favourable consideration to the passing of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Bill No. S-15, an act to incorporate the Good News Broadcasting Association of Canada, raises a number of questions. Is it a new Christian sect? Is it necessary to introduce a bill in the house when a member rises and says that this association is already preaching the Christian doctrine in Canada? That is precisely the point which I do not particularly like.
Private Bills
In fact, quite often in the house, we are told: It does not matter whether you accept the bill or not, the corporation is already in operation in Canada.
Now, what are the aims of the said corporation? Section 4 states:
The objects of the corporation shall be
(a)	to promote the dissemination of Christian knowledge and to promote, organize, establish, maintain and carry on, conduct and assist organizations or facilities for the dissemination of Christian knowledge in all its branches and activities, including foreign and home missions, publishing houses, seminaries, schools, colleges, public correspondence schools, hospitals, dispensaries, parsonages, orphanages and homes for the aged, and any other institutions and organizations for charitable purposes or any of them;
(b)	to supply and render charitable services to poor and needy persons.
At this stage, Mr. Chairman, one is justified to wonder whether this is an organization similar to the Salvation Army?
Is the activity of this corporation a duplication of that of the Salvation Army, which I will admit, renders tremendous services in all parts of Canada?
Paragraphs (c) and (d) of section 4 read as follows:
(c)	to give and to receive donations for charitable purposes and in connection therewith to do all things reasonably necessary in order to comply with any terms stipulated by the donors of gifts made from time to time to the corporation; and
(d)	to do all such other things as are incidental or conducive to the attainment of the above objects.
Mr. Chairman, the primary question, I believe, is to know since when this organization has been operating in Canada, in what provinces, and through what radio stations.
I understand that the headquarters of the corporation are located in Winnipeg, but it is always dangerous for us, in parliament, to pass legislation to give the right to receive donations for charitable purposes.
Quite often, so-called charity organizations were created here and there in Canada, but then people found they were organized rackets more than anything else.
I should not like this bill to make it possible for an organization of three or four men to form another racket.
If its purpose is to promote Christian doctrine, is it a new religion or is it just an organization like the Salvation Army that we are being asked to authorize in Canada? If so, I would say that our country already has numerous organizations to look after the poor and the destitute, in other words all those who suffer.
Mr. Chairman, if that organization is already operating in Canada, as the hon. member has stated a while ago, why is this bill presented to us and why are we told

"Whether you pass it or not, the organization will continue its operations just the same".
I feel we should have more information. We need explanations concerning the set-up of that organization and the number of years it has been in Canada or in the western provinces.

First I should like to make a few comments on organization before I pinpoint the particular needs of Kootenay West. I thought that the royal commission on government organization made a few excellent recommendations, and I agree with them as a result of my own experience. I am going to deal with three or four of them particularly with respect to the purchase of property, the inventory required to know what property we have in Canada, and the management of property.
The first one was that consideration be given to consolidating, in a single statute, land legislation having general application to the acquisition by purchase or lease, and the disposal or leasing to others, of real property in Canada and abroad by all departments and agencies of the crown. I think that recommendation merits further consideration because I have noticed a growing need for this approach as the years go by.
The second recommendation was that the Department of Public Works be made responsible for the development of a complete inventory of properties owned or leased by the federal government and its agencies, and its maintenance as a perpetual record by posting to it all future acquisitions and disposals as they occur. I think that is an excellent suggestion so that we will know in total what our assets in public property are and what disposals have occurred throughout the year. There is some tightening up needed. I am speaking from local experiences on a very small scale but they do indicate the need for consideration of this recommendation.
The third was that the Department of Public Works, in its organization for real property management, assign staff to be responsible for land use aspects of federal property ownership and to consult and cooperate with other levels of government and their agencies for the future development of urban, rural and regional areas. There has been a big improvement in the last ten years with respect to property management in the property management division. You do not go into a public building nowadays as you might have ten or 12 years ago and find that nobody knows who is in charge. At that time you would find the janitor fighting with the postmaster as to who was in charge of

the building and problems of that sort. There is a greatly improved state of affairs there.
Perhaps it should be the janitor.

Yes, that is quite correct, and rightly so. When a man is managing a building he should be in charge. But I have seen quite a contest between the district architect, the janitor and the postmaster as to who was in charge of a federal public building. These things are being cleared up.
There is a very interesting recommendation with respect to the need for decentralization and field organization. There has been a lot done in that direction but I think there could be more done. This is what the report has to say:
The extent to which future activities of the Department of Public Works should be decentralized cannot be categorically stated at this time. While in general there are obvious advantages in transferring to the field certain operational functions and thereby improving the efficiency with which the needs of client departments and agencies in the field may be met, the extent to which the user departments themselves delegate authority to the field has a direct bearing upon what may be appropriate. Based on experience elsewhere, your commissioners believe that a fairly substantial delegation of authority to responsible offices, each with such satellites as may be required, will probably prove most satisfactory.
I mention that because throughout the years I have been informed there have been occasions when the district office or local people had to refer to Ottawa with respect to calling for tenders for piling, tenders for lumber or tenders for wharf floats or something of that sort and there has been unnecessary delay. If the people on the ground are competent they know better than anyone else which is the best purchase to make and which is the best value. There have been delays to such an extent that on one or two occasions the building of wharves was delayed until the next season because of rising water, and so on. I trust as a result of the recommendations of the commission on government organization, and the experience of the department, the minister will realize the need for a continuation of the district office in the Koote-nays. There has been some suggestion that because steamer service has disappeared from the rivers, there is no necessity for a local office. I want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that we have a different type of traffic now. We have a large number of tugs towing timber. We have a great increase in pleasure craft. There is a need for a continuation of an office because of the requirement for the building and maintenance of wharves, the dredging of rivers, the placing of piles and everything that is necessary to carry on navigation successfully. I urge that

consideration be given to the retention of the office in Nelson to serve the Okanagan and Kootenay areas.
I have one other suggestion that has to do with public relations. The report says:
The reticence of many departments in publicizing their activities through the press inhibits the development of groups of specialists for this purpose. The Department of Public Works construction programs are frequently of intense local interest across Canada, but it had no organized information service until 1954-
I believe that is about the time Mr. Winters took over and General Young became deputy minister.
-and the unit then inaugurated has been kept to a modest size. In the Department of Defence Production, which is a comparable source of frequent but low-keyed news, press releases and other necessary information services are under the direct supervision of the deputy minister.
When relations with the news services are retained in the deputy minister, it is generally good practice to designate the responsible member of his staff by name, even if the duties are too light to justify a full time appointment. This is a convenience to the press and a safeguard against uncertainties and confusion within the department. For such an appointment, some knowledge of information techniques is desirable but not imperative; of greater importance is an intimate knowledge of policies and operations.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in that connection I do urge the necessity for the improvement of the public relations of the department, not necessarily for the advantage of the department, however I believe that when interesting works are being built or interesting developments are taking place there should be an official press release from the department concerned, so that everybody knows exactly what is happening. You would be amazed how interested the people in these districts are in public works projects.
I urge the necessity for senior officials, when visiting the districts in connection with projects of importance, communicating with local organizations as well. They will get sound advice from local organizations. I found, on a number of occasions throughout the years, quite serious blunders had been made and then later, because of contact with local organizations, quite serious blunders have been avoided. I should like to give one or two illustrations of this point. I understand that the department and the district architect have been giving consideration to some alterations to the Gray building in Nelson, which is a federal public building in which the post office and other departments are housed. The sea cadets have been using the basement, and found it very useful indeed. Then, they heard that civil defence was going to take over. They were going to put in some windows, some ventilation and make some other changes. They heard other organizations were
Supply-Public Works
going to use this basement. Now, in order to avoid all this concern on the part of the navy league, the sea cadets, the city council and others who, like most organizations in Kootenay West, get in touch with their member to try to find out what is going on, there should have been some information given by the architect when he was visiting the district. He could have called three or four people together and said, "We are going to redesign the basement, but you need not be worried. As soon as it is done you will all be fitted in again." This procedure would have avoided a lot of concern.
Then, there is the question of sites for local post offices and other buildings. No one knows more about local conditions than the local people. I have had an illustration recently of a district architect choosing a site on a side-street in a small village. He may have had very good reasons for doing so, but there have been complaints about it. The parliamentary secretary is having the matter looked into, and he very kindly wrote to me to tell me the district architect was going to visit this small village, meet the local business people, and so on. I think it would be a good idea to do that before any final decision is made, and then the decision will be satisfactory all around.
I recall when the question of wharves came up on one occasion, and some $4,000 was being appropriated to dismantle a certain wharf. I know all these wharves and their condition. This was a sound wharf, good for another 20 years. It had good piling and good decking, and $4,000 was to be spent to destroy it. The local people in the district said they did not need it for the stern wheelers, but that about a hundred pleasure craft came up from Portland and other points north during the summer. This is the best 300-mile inland water trip in America. Some of these pleasure craft would stop at this wharf, which was going to be destroyed. The people got in touch with me and I said to the minister, why not spend that $4,000 in repairing the wharf? This was done, and so we have a sound and useful wharf which will last another 20 years.
This type of situation does not happen when the local organizations are consulted. This usually happens when someone comes from outside who does not know the people, is not used to dropping in and visiting the local storekeepers, and so on. These little courtesies make for co-operation.
In so far as dredging is concerned, if you want to know what dredging is required on the Columbia river, the Arrow lakes or the other waterways, the officials should keep in touch with the captains of the vessels that

Supply-Public Works
are operating on the lakes. They know where the shoals occur, and where the levels change with high and low water. The department should seek their advice and would quite often be able to avoid unnecessary checking. However, I have very little criticism in this respect. Years ago, and up to recent years, the men who visited the area would make a trip on a tug for a hundred miles or so, just to see how the channels were. I do suggest that this type of co-operation does not cost much, but it does add to the efficiency of the department and the appreciation of the work it is doing.
There is one other question I should like to mention. In the interior of British Columbia, and I suppose the same condition exists in a good many places, the department depends on a large percentage of so-called casual employees. In a good number of cases, these casual employees have worked for the department for 20 or 25 years, especially in dredging or on the docks. They are laid off when the water starts to rise and they are re-employed when the water goes down and dredging can begin. Throughout the years there has been some extra work found for some of them in the maintenance of wharves, and so on.
I know that in one case the question of this labour was raised and they built a wharf for some $4,000 less than the estimated cost by contract. I suggest that consideration be given to keeping these very competent men employed as long as possible each year. You cannot replace them nowadays. They are used to running pile drivers, handling equipment for the building of wharves, running dredges and things of that sort. They are particularly skilled, in so far as that district is concerned, because of their knowledge of the channels in the waterways and so on. I suggest that every effort be made to continue their employment as long as possible by planning the work so that when dredging is over they can be employed on wharf construction or wharf maintenance.
I should like now to say a word or two about architecture. I am interested in all types of architecture, mobile and immobile, Mr. Chairman. I recognize the need for functional construction. The first consideration has to be functional design in the erection of a building. I suggest that the time has come when some consideration should be given to developing types of architecture appropriate to the region in which the buildings are to be erected. A building that is appropriate on the prairies is not necessarily appropriate in the mountainous areas of B.C. One of these flat California-type buildings on the prairies fits into the landscape, with its horizontal

lines, but it looks completely out of place if it is backed against two very steep mountain sides. I am not going to say very much about that, but I am very interested in architecture and I think more consideration should be given to designs appropriate to the regions in which buildings are to be erected.
Some mention was made of the role of the department and that it should be, as it were, an economic buffer in our society. Road work has been an economic buffer ever since Canada was established. In the early days people used to pay their taxes with road work, and later they got cash for it. I remember in the early days of this century you would not get work on the roads if you did not belong to the Conservative association. Then when the Liberals got in, you had to belong to the Liberal association to get work. That has all disappeared now. There is no patronage in my district. I have not seen any of that sort of thing for many years. There is great scope for the department to act as an economic buffer, particularly to provide winter employment on heavy rock work and bridge construction when the work is undertaken as a result of long term planning; but I warn that it is not possible to do this planning successfully on a year to year basis.
I cannot help saying a word or two about the trans-Canada highway. I know some of my colleagues do not agree with me in this connection, and we have different views as to where the second highway should be. However, I am going to suggest that every consideration be given to the development of the southern provincial highway as the second trans-Canada highway in British Columbia, because it goes through the most populated area of British Columbia and where the greatest proportion of the wealth of the province is produced.
Now, I come to a few local things in my constituency. I am only mentioning a few because I am expecting to see the minister out there soon and we will give him a good time, like we do with everybody, who visits us, and show him around.
If we all did this we would be here for years and years.
Pardon?
If we all did this, touched on local topics, we would go on for years.

Mr. Chairman, surely the hon. gentleman does not deny the hon. member for Kootenay West the right to place representations before the minister that he has promised his constituents he would place before him. I just make a few suggestions. I think consideration should be given to the deeper dredging and the widening of the

channel going into the wharf at Arrowhead at the head of the Arrow lakes, and also going into the Columbia river. We had a number of pleasure craft from Portland there last year and some got stuck on the shoals. Some dredging is necessary at the mouth of the river also, and some improvement in the navigation markers and so on.
I hope the improvements to the Gray building in Nelson will soon be undertaken so that civil defence members, the sea cadets and others can carry on as usual. Some further dredging and rip-rap are required at the narrows between the upper and lower lakes on the Columbia river, and I hope the minister will give favourable consideration to providing a launching ramp at Trout lake. There are only a few permanent residents there, but it has a big summer population and its principal income is from the tourist business. Whenever it is considered necessary to replace a wharf or remove a wharf the local people should be consulted, because very often these wharves, by cutting them in half, can be converted into launching ramps suitable for small pleasure craft.
I also want to bring the minister's attention to the fact that there is a necessity for a new 6torm boom around the launching ramp at a place called Boswell, and once again I emphasize the necessity for consultation with local organizations and local people who know their communities' requirements and have a knowledge of local circumstances and river conditions.
In view of the threatened Columbia river development, I wish to ask the minister, has any survey been made of the wharves that would be flooded, and have estimates been made of the cost of rebuilding these facilities between Castlegar and Revelstoke? I am sure the cost would run into hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Another matter is the question of snow removal. Many wharves are on a 10 per cent grade, and if they are not sanded in winter they can be quite dangerous. There have been cases of difference of opinion as to whether a certain wharf was the responsibility of the federal government or the provincial government. 1 bring that to the minister's attention because it can be very serious when you have 20 or 30 cars going over an icy dock. I ask that the responsibility for snow removal be determined for every dock, before the winter season commences.
Mr. Chairman, I find a little restlessness on my right. I seldom rise in this house-
The understatement of the year.

-but now my concluding inquiry is this-
Supply-Public Works
Hear, hear.

I appreciate the applause I am getting from all sides. There have been some recent press references with respect to the restoration of lovers' lane to its former beauty and usefulness. In view of the unusual interest in Ottawa in this project, I would appreciate the minister informing the house of his department's plans in this respect. This restoration has been contemplated for many years and I have had a number of phone calls about it recently. I do hope the minister tell us what his plans are for lovers' lane.

Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure to follow the hon. member for Kootenay West and because I want to save the time of the committee I simply say I ratify and confirm his preliminary remarks with regard to the minister and his staff, save with respect to such part of the statement he made having reference to the constituency of Kootenay West, because after listening to the hon. member for six years I have come to the conclusion that short of Heaven no land could be as fair, nor no people as amiable as those who inhabit the constituency of Kootenay West.
Now, I will come directly to one specific issue, and I have already advised the minister of the matter with which I intend to deal. It is the situation apropos of the construction on the Peace river, in the vicinity of Hudson Hope, of a very large hydroelectric project involving the damming of the river and the ultimate setting up of a reservoir which will extend back over the channel of the Peace and up the Rocky mountain trench for several hundred miles.
As I assess the situation by an examination of the facts and the pertinent legislation, I can only say it would appear that the province of British Columbia is proceeding with this project in complete breach and in defiance of the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and that this government is indulging in a studied ignorance of this particular breach of the law. From time to time I have put several questions on the order paper, and up until several weeks ago the minister, in response to a question I put to him, said that no application for approval of this particular project had been received by him as the minister charged with responsibility under this particular act.
A short time after that, so that there should be no doubt about the matter, I asked the Minister of Justice whether in the opinion of the officials of his department this particular project was one which was covered by the provisions of this legislation. The minister replied to me on October 14 that the advice he had received was to the

Supply-Public Works
effect that the works in question were included in the class of works to which the Navigable Waters Protection Act applies. This simply confirms the research I made, the cases I studied and my understanding of what is concerned in this particular project. I make it quite plain, Mr. Chairman, that so far as I am concerned and the people in my country, we have no objection to this project and we have always given due credit to the government of British Columbia for proceeding with it. We feel it will serve a great need now and in the future to satisfy the hunger for electricity which will, I think, be greatly intensified in the southern parts of British Columbia and in the Pacific northwest. But there is a statute, and the thousands of people who live below where the project is planned along the Peace river are entitled, if there is a law and it is a good law, to ask that it be observed by the government of British Columbia, and that the federal government make certain that there is due observance of the statute. The statute is very simple. Section 4 of the act says:
No work shall be built or placed in, upon, over, under, through or across any navigable water unless the site and plans thereof have been approved by the minister; and the work is built, placed and maintained in accordance with the plans and the regulations.
Then the act goes on to provide that a publication shall be made in the Canada Gazette and in two newspapers circulated in the district. I ask the minister now whether since I last spoke to him or directed any questions to him there has been an application for approval filed on behalf of the province of British Columbia, even though it is long overdue and there has been this breach of the legislation in the interval. I will be glad to resume my seat in the belief that this matter will be dealt with in due course, if such an application has been received. If one has not been received, I would like to proceed with the matter. Can the minister say whether any such application has been received?
No application has been received, Mr. Chairman.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I put this to the minister and to the members of this committee. This project, as I understand it, will involve the filling of this reservoir, which may take a period of 8, 10, or 12, or possibly even 14 years, depending on the run-off and the amount of water available. During that period the province of British Columbia, or the authority which is acting on behalf of the province, will have complete control-without having filed any plans, as it should have filed plans, as to what is proposed by its engineering plans with regard to this
[Mr. Baldwin.}
program-will be diverting water and will be interfering with the navigability of the Peace river. This river has been navigated from the time of Alexander Mackenzie, who in 1799 was the first white man to reach the Pacific coast from overland. The first trip I made on the Peace river in 1929 was on a boat which accommodated several hundred people. I have no doubt

at least I would so hope-that the engineering plans of the province of British Columbia are proper and suitable plans and will take into consideration the requirements of the people who live downstream.
I might only say here, sir, that I am informed that some time ago a departmental committee was established of different departments of this government-or it might have been of the previous government-to examine the extent to which this interference and diversion of the waters of the Peace might affect the navigation in the Mackenzie river area. The Peace flows into Slave river, thence into Great Slave lake, from which the Mackenzie emerges and flows to the Arctic. I do not know whether this committee has completed its deliberations and I do not know what results have been produced. But we have heard in the last few weeks, apart altogether from the question of navigation, the potentially serious situation which might develop in Canada as it has developed in the United States with regard to this question of the use of waters and large rivers.
I think it quite wrong, quite improper, that under these conditions the government of British Columbia has not seen fit to file its plans. There is an obvious recognition that this is a river in respect of which application should be filed, because I have here under the date January 26, 1963, an extract from the Canada Gazette which is a notice by the government of the province of British Columbia, through the minister of highways, that there has been deposited with the Minister of Public Works in Ottawa, under this cut, and filed in the office of the district registrar of the land registry district of Kamloops, a description of site and plan of a highway bridge proposed to be built across the Peace river near Hudson Hope. This, as I understand it, is a highway bridge to be used in conjunction with this project. I may be wrong in that, but that is my understanding.
Let me conclude, Mr. Chairman, by saying that I had occasion not so many years ago to be concerned in the case of a small farmer who had purchased land on the south shore of Lesser Slave lake and through whose land flowed a small stream which at certain seasons of the year was barely navigable. A fisherman who plied his trade in the Lesser Slave lake area wanted, on possibly three

or four occasions in the year, to pass through this stream into the lake. The farmer had fenced this land and he was compelled, as a result of proceedings initiated by the Department of Public Works, to take down his fence. He was later assessed damages as a result of an action brought in the exchequer court. There is no doubt in the world that this type of work falls within the four corners of this legislation.
My submission is that if this is a good law- and I am satisfied it is a good law-it should apply to the rich as well as to the poor, to the strong as well as to the weak; and it would be my hope that before next spring comes around the government of the province of British Columbia will have purged its defiance of this legislation and will have filed its plans and will, I hope, proceed properly and to the satisfaction of the people of this country with this project-but under the law, and not above the law.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few very brief words about this difficult matter of selecting projects. We have heard tonight about a very large number of small projects, particularly projects in Kootenay West. We have heard about one very large project in northern British Columbia. There are projects all over the country of different characters, with different advantages and different costs, and this presents a very difficult problem of selection. In the United States and in some countries overseas this problem has been tackled on a reasonably sound basis. The type of analysis which has now begun to be reported extensively in the text books is generally described as benefit-cost analysis.
By and large this approach looks ahead over many years. It puts under one heading the benefits and on the other side of the ledger the costs. The benefits are assessed by the economists, who look ahead at the various requirements. They may be a single need or they may be several needs in the case of a multi-purpose project. These are evaluated in dollar terms. These are the incomes, the revenues, the benefits of the project in question. Then on the opposite side of the ledger are the costs. The costs are assessed essentially by the engineers but they may be reduced, for example, if there is a large pocket of unemployed in the area and the expenditure, for instance, by the federal government in respect of unemployment insurance is reduced.
There are, in other words, a variety of considerations to be taken into account with respect to cost. A project is basically economic if the benefits over many years, paid for in accordance with today's values, are greater than the costs. This does not mean
Supply-Public Works
that a project should always go ahead. Various alternatives should be studied and the project which has the highest ratio of benefits to costs is the one which deserves the highest priority. I confidently expect that with the passage of time more projects will be evaluated in this way in different parts of the country. Adoption of this method would mean that more objective and independent decisions will be made in deciding which are the most economic projects. It would mean that those with the greatest social as well as the greatest economic advantages would go ahead first. The most persuasive member might not manage to get as many buildings or other projects in his area, but the national interest would be better served if such an objective appraisal were made.
We have in the last few years made some progress along these lines in Canada. We now have a publication entitled "A guide to benefit cost analysis" whose production was one of the results of the resources for tomorrow conference. It is available to all government departments and it is now being used, I understand, in the Department of Public Works. It is certainly being used in various government departments in the provinces and I trust that in the future it will be used even more widely. I think there will be less controversy and less politics involved in establishing priorities and that, in the long run, it would lead to greater national advantage if this were the case. I certainly suggest to the minister that it be used more extensively than it is now in the Department of Public Works.

I wonder if the hon. member would agree-I am sure he wants to be fair about this-that the booklet to which he referred arose out of the deliberations of some of those who were brought to Ottawa at the instance of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle when he was minister and that the proposal for liaison between provincial ministers was also one of the ideas brought forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I thought the hon. member might care to comment on this in case one of his hon. friends later on might want to claim that this is a creation of the present government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: I will be glad to do so. Certainly, the resources for tomorrow conference was a product of the previous administration, perhaps one of its best accomplishments. I would say further, though, that a number of us from across the country participated, and as one of the authors of this book I advocate its extensive use throughout the country.

It is not my wish to speak at great length and unduly delay the minister's

Supply-Public Works
estimates. However, this is the first opportunity I have had to publicly congratulate him upon his elevation to the cabinet, and I know that his years of experience in the house will enable him to carry out his duties in a fair and impartial manner so as to bring credit to him and his department.
I am sure all of us were pleased to learn that it is the intention of the hon. gentleman and of this government to continue the winter works program established by the Conservative government. It is said that imitation is the sincerest form of flattery and, certainly, the recent announcement that the government intends to proceed with the program to construct adequate post offices for rural areas will meet with general approval among Canadians. This program of post office construction began as a result of a federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa on July 14 and 15, 1958-a conference attended by nine provincial labour ministers, beside representatives of management, labour and various municipalities across Canada.
The winter works program is available to every municipality wishing to take advantage of it, and since it is a truly national cooperative effort I believe it is one which might very well be carried on every winter. In fact, it is gratifying to us on this side of the house to see the present government adopting a "me too" policy in so many fields. Not only is it continuing our winter works program, but it is carrying on with our program of providing aid for home construction through the central mortgage and housing corporation, it is continuing to use the devalued dollar, it is continuing to support the building of technical training schools so as to provide new skills for those who are unemployed; it has adopted our shipbuilding program and many other projects which were initiated in 1958 and 1959 when it became evident this country needed policies which would guide its great leap forward into the age of automation. These policies and programs were initiated by the then Conservative government.
Among the programs begun in 1958 was a scheme for the building of small post offices across Canada. I well remember, when I was first elected in 1957, visiting the post offices in New Ross, Lunenburg county, and Brooklyn in Queens county, and conditions in those offices were deplorable. It was evident to me at that time that the former Liberal administration had lost touch with the people, for little or no thought had been given to providing adequate buildings for this necessary public service. We realized of course, that something had to be done, and we initiated a crash program which saw 70 new post offices started across Canada in 1959. Not only did these offices lead to the provision of better 
facilities, but work on their construction contributed to easing the unemployment problem which plagued our government-a problem which still faces us today. We have at the present time well over a quarter of a million people unemployed in Canada and the government has yet to give us any indication of its plans to create full employment.
The recent announcement in Queens-Lunen-burg that seven new post offices would be built is, of course, helpful. I am pleased to note that my request to the minister that every consideration be given to the needs of my constituents has fallen on such fruitful ground, as far as post offices are concerned. The minister is, of course, free to make these announcements in any manner that pleases him but I would have thought, in view of the friendly relations which exist between us, that he would have released this information through the elected member of parliament rather than through a spokesman for the Liberal party. In any event, the beneficiaries of this extended Conservative program are the people of Queens county and Lunenburg county, and I can assure the minister that regardless of the manner in which these announcements are made any project which will be of benefit to my constituents would be most welcome.
There are a number of questions which come to my mind. I am wondering whether these post offices will be built under the terms of the winter works incentive program, whether they will be constructed in the usual way and provided for in the estimates, or whether the spokesman on this occasion had some advance knowledge concerning next years estimates. This is a question I should like the minister to answer if he has time.
I should like to suggest that, when considering the erection of new public buildings, the minister should give some thought to the needs of the people in Bridgewater, Nova Scotia. At the present time the various agencies of the government are located in different buildings throughout the town. This creates difficulties for the citizens who must use these various services, as well as for the employed personnel. In Lunenburg, for example, we have a new public building and in this building provision has been made for officials of the fisheries department as well as for officers of the customs branch, officials of the unemployment insurance commission and the post office. This is a very desirable situation from the point of view of the public in that certain economies are effected with a consolidation of various services. This is the type of federal building required in Bridgewater. Here we have a town that is growing

rapidly, it is the shopping centre of Lunenburg county serving a large agricultural area. The present facilities are overcrowded and inadequate, and I would urge upon the minister the need for carrying out a survey with the hope that a larger federal building, capable of housing all the government offices in Bridgewater, will be built in the near future.
I am also concerned with the minister's plans for a bridge over the canal at Chester, in Lunenburg county. We have in Nova Scotia only two canals. One of these is located at St. Peters in Cape Breton; the other is located in my riding at Chester. During the past summer the walls of this canal collapsed. Although it is still possible for small craft to proceed through the canal, it is evident that something of a permanent nature must be done to repair the damage that has been caused. The last plans I heard of from the department were to the effect that they would fill in the canal and at some future date would then dredge out this filling and build an adequate bridge to carry the traffic which must proceed from the town of Chester to the peninsula. However, to date no action has been taken in this matter. A temporary bridge has been built across the canal, but I am informed that this is inadequate to carry heavy trucks and that the people living on the peninsula are very much concerned in the event that a fire should occur; for there is the possibility that the existing temporary bridge could not carry a fire engine. Therefore I would ask the minister to give careful consideration to doing something about providing a suitable bridge over the damaged canal at Chester.
I could mention many other matters, Mr. Chairman, but I see that time is running out. However, one item I should like to bring to the minister's attention is the need for a further harbour development in Liverpool, in Queens county. This home of privateers in by-gone days is today showing new resurgence and growth. Formerly the wharves and docking facilities were adequate for the fishermen, but the shipbuilding program of the Conservative government has changed all this. Today the fishermen are building larger draggers and trawlers. In fact, the firm of Steel and Engine Products Limited at Liverpool recently completed the first steel stern trawler to be built in Nova Scotia. This new development has created two problems. The present harbour is not deep enough in certain areas to accommodate the growing fleet; and the present wharf at Liverpool should be lengthened by at least 300 feet to provide additional docking space for the new and growing fleet of fishing trawlers. I hope the
Supply-Public Works
minister will give immediate consideration to this problem so that the development of this primary industry in Queens county will in no way be curtailed.

Mr. Chairman, consideration of the estimates of the various departments always results in interesting debates, and today's discussion has been all the more interesting because, in my opinion, it deals with a department whose action is felt immediately by the whole economy, stimulating as it does the activities in several fields.
The presentation of the estimates of the Minister of Public Works goes back to last October 18. At that time, he made a short statement, too short in my opinion, about his plans. There again, the word may not be right because in fact they are plans drawn up by the previous government and to which he made only minor changes. However, we were happy to read in Hansard that he expected his estimates to show a substantial increase next year.
We heard him say those same things a while ago. Of course that does not give much to all those who put their faith in the candidates of the present government during the last elections, hoping that they would look after problems immediately.
When he presented his estimates last October 18, he said he hoped to direct his department for at least 20 years. I am very happy to see that he has such good intentions. If through his work, his persistence, initiative and success, he reaches his objectives, the Canadian people will benefit from that desire because if he wants to remain in office that long he will have to show himself worthy of it through the efficiency of the means used to further his department's business.
I read with great interest the debate of October 18. There were very interesting discussions during which good suggestions were made by members of the opposition. Allegations and even charges were made against a certain type of patronage reportedly being practised at the present time in the Department of Public Works. But these charges were denied by the minister, and I was very pleased to hear that. A document dating back to 1954 was even tabled at that time. If nothing more recent can be found, I feel that the problem is not as serious as suggested, and surely the minister cannot be blamed for the situation prevailing at that time.
Besides, I have no intention of defending the minister at all. I am well aware that he can defend for himself, but I cannot resist the temptation to quote these words from the holy scriptures:

Supply-Public Works
Let he who is without sin cast the first stone at him.
If these words were applied, I am sure that the accusations would come only from one corner of the house.
In any event, we know that there is a great danger of patronage in the Department of Public Works, where opportunities are perhaps more numerous than anywhere else. We take the liberty of urging the minister to use every means at his disposal to preserve us against that distressing evil.
We agree that defeated candidates of political parties deserve some recognition from the group they represented, but such party recognition should not be shown at the expense of the Canadian people or opposition members, because those members do represent the majority of voters in their ridings.
The Department of Public Works is extending its activities in many fields and on that basis, it is of vital importance in the economic life of the country. In my opinion, a budget of less than $200 million is much too small to enable the department to play its rightful part.
Everybody will agree that the money available is far from sufficient to enable the department to meet even the most urgent requirements.
As a matter of fact, a very simple calculation indicates that the budget of public works is only 2.8 per cent of the total budget. Such a percentage is definitely inadequate, considering all the responsibilities of that department.
In my opinion, that department could act as a stabilizer in the country's economy by maintaining in various parts of the country permanent work sites or development works of all kinds, capable of absorbing a certain proportion of the labour force unemployed at present or likely to become unemployed.
The minister also referred a while ago to this pet project of his and I hope that he will obtain the necessary co-operation from the cabinet to carry out this plan.
The needs of Canada are great. In a vast and young country such as ours, everything must be done, and considering the direction which seems to be taken by the present government, it is quite logical, in my opinion, that it should undertake and carry out an extensive program of public works which would provide work for the great number of unemployed.
As for us in the province of Quebec, this evil is still more acute than elsewhere. And surely there is no lack of needs.
The St. Lawrence river crossing the entire province is our pride and at the same time a vehicle for materials which we greatly

appreciate. On the other hand, many dredging, cleaning, digging and development works are essential to maintain the seaway which is increasingly used. Traffic being heavier, it should be improved to speed it up.
I think I need not remind members of the committee and the minister of the accidents which occurred lately on the St. Lawrence to underline the urgency of certain work on this important seaway.
More and more, the shores of the St. Lawrence river are being lined with summer cottages and permanent homes, which means that retaining walls have to be erected as protection measures against tides, ice or damage due to navigation.
Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out to the minister that the building of retaining walls to check erosion of certain pieces of land, is an urgent matter, for heavy damage is caused to this land every year due to ice, tides or navigation.
Mr. Chairman, I represent a riding which is particularly affected by that problem. I get numerous requests concerning the building of those walls. Each time, we have to engage in discussions-not to say in a battle- with the engineers of the department in order to determine who is responsible for the damage done and ask the minister to intervene personally to speed up the investigations, etc., etc.
Far be it from me, however, to accuse the officers of the department of being incompetent or of working against the interests of the taxpayers. On the contrary, those to whom I addressed myself have always proved themselves to be quite competent and have shown a lot of good will. But those people, as I can well understand, work under particularly difficult circumstances and conditions and, not having the credit required to carry out the work, they are faced with the famous dilemma: either to recommend that the work be postponed or simply to refuse the job completely.
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt about it, Portneuf is a beautiful riding that I am proud to represent. The area is greatly appreciated by tourists, who always like to go back there.
I do not want to insist, but I feel duty bound to ask at this time for special projects precisely to help my constituency to keep this high reputation. Numerous projects have already been carried out, others are being completed, and I wish to thank the people responsible for that. However, there are still many gaps to fill. I call the minister's attention on that situation.
The Department of Public Works is also responsible for the construction of public buildings. If each member of the committee

were asked to state the needs of his riding, I am sure everyone would have something to say and we would be sitting here for quite a while. That goes to show that the needs are both urgent and numerous.
If buildings were erected to meet the present needs and, naturally, if the necessary funds were available, it would be possible to provide work for thousands of men in the building trades and thousands more in the building materials industry. That would somewhat palliate the disastrous effect of the famous 4, 8 or 11 per cent tax, call it whatever you want.
Mr. Chairman, the people who belong to the building trades are particularly dear to me. It may be because I am one of them. I should add though that a major part of my riding's economy depends on the building materials industry.
Wood as such or transformed into wall panels or plywood provides the livelihood of thousands of people. Hundreds of others work in my constituency's stone or granite quarries which are, in fact, the most important in Canada. Many others are directly interested in the building trades, to say nothing of the people who produce or prepare cement, this all-important building material.
All those people I have the honour to represent, regardless of party affiliation, insist that I submit their requests to the house.
Those people like their work; they have their own homes and lead an active social life. They wish to stay in their respective parishes, near their relatives and friends.
Of those thousands of workers, each and every one has felt at various degrees, the harmful effect of the tax on building materials.
At present, hundreds of unemployed live in anxiety and fear for the future. Many of them did not even succeed in accumulating enough unemployment insurance stamps during the summer and must now be content with small unemployment assistance benefits.
For all those reasons and many others and because I represent a group of workers, I would ask the Minister of Public Works to see to it that his department launch immediately a vast program of public works which would constitute a market for the building materials produced by some of my constituents and also a labour market for the workers who are available and who are willing to work.
The responsibility for the success of the Canadian world exhibition rests for the most part with the Minister of Public Works. We believe that the forecasts for this event are of primary importance to the Canadian people
Supply-Public Works
and give us a particularly well chosen opportunity to apply a vast program of work which could efficiently lessen the problems of the unemployed, provided, however, that the money so employed is not wasted, as is the case now.
Of course, we believe that the choice of the Montreal area is a happy one, and we commend that initiative on the part of the authorities who made the decision. But we must nevertheless express surprise at the fact that an island has to be built on the river to have an appropriate site for this exhibition. It appeared to us laymen that it would have been easy to locate this exhibition on the shore, without having to build an artificial island.
During consideration of the estimates of the Department of National Defence, a few days ago, numerous protests have been made following the announcement of reductions in that department. And the same word always comes back: unemployment. We do not dispute the fact that $74 million have been saved, but we are concerned, and justly so, about the repercussions such a saving may have on the unemployment situation.
Mr. Chairman, millions of dollars have been distributed among Canadian citizens, each year, in unemployment assistance and social assistance of all kinds. We certainly recognize that those sums of money made it possible for some families to live, but we believe that this money fills only half its purpose and that if the federal government, together with the provinces and the municipalities, were making this capital work by investing it in public projects, we would decrease the number of the needy in two ways, first by giving work to a large number of them, and second, by maintaining the operation of the industries which manufacture the products needed for the implementation of such work.
If we succeed, during and because of a war, to set up powerful enterprises, I believe more firmly still that the establishing of peacetime industries is not only feasible, but indeed desirable and advisable.
Mr. Chairman, one of my former teachers, Commander Beauge, launched, many years ago, a bold project which, at the time, seemed utopian and impracticable, but which could now be easily carried out owing to the scientific and engineering strides of our era. Everybody guessed it and I think the hon. member for Saguenay (Mr. Blouin) even mentioned it in the house during the last session. I am referring to the project of the construction of a dam between Newfoundland and Labrador which would completely change nearly half the country's economy because of its effects on the climate.

Supply-Public Works
Such a project might make you smile at first sight, but I am sure that if the minister could afford it, he would be very happy to carry it out because I think that is a project worthy of him.
Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted at this time to point out to the house a notice of motion which was introduced by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Mar-coux) and which particularly concerns the activity of the public works department. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I shall read that notice of motion in order to draw the minister's attention to the problems involved.
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of taking steps to provide a plan whereby, in cases where over $50,000 is to be spent on constructing or renovating buildings belonging to the government, under the administration and management of the Department of Public Works or any other department at home or abroad, 1 per cent of the amount should be allocated for artistic work such as murals, sculptures, ornamental walls, flooring, mosaic work, frescoes, tapestries, paintings, fountains, lighting fixtures and other similar work, and that all such work be conceived and executed by Canadian artists; and, to provide further that such artists should work in co-operation with the architects in charge of the construction in order to bring about the closest possible integration; and further, that a competent and independent board be set up by the Canada Council to allocate the contracts fairly among the artists, and to ensure that all aspects of any such program are observed and implemented.
Mr. Chairman, I think that suggestion should be taken into consideration and to me, it looks like very proper action which would benefit our Canadian artists and would be an incentive for them to develop the renown of our country in the arts.
