Mr. Chairman, during my remarks, I suggested several important projects. I realize the minister could not carry them out at the present time because of the limitations he must take into consideration in performing his duties, which necessarily involve a lack of credit.
Of course, to carry out these projects, considerable amount of money will be necessary. But if we consider the saturation point reached by the taxation burden, we realize that we shall have to seek the necessary credits elsewhere.
Our solution, on this side of the house, obviously appears too simple to some, while others find it too complicated; but I feel that the economists of the party in power should suggest a gradual adoption of these economic measures advocated by us, that is to say the creation of new, interest-free credit, as our economy is able to absorb it.
I am not astonished to see that some of our hon. friends opposite are smiling; but if they want me to lose what I call my illusions, let them find some other solution.
[Mr. Frenette.l
Actually, I do not believe in the spontaneous generating of limitless amounts of credit, but I stick to the idea that the infusion of new capital, through the Bank of Canada, into well ordered channels, is the only solution available to us. All other possible means have been tried, and they brought about the present situation. That is why I suggest that we adapt our financial system to our most urgent needs. Let us be up to date.
If this were done, I feel that the minister could fulfil his task adequately and, by so doing, have the wish expressed on the memorable evening of October 18, 1963, when he said he would like to remain at the head of his department for the next 20 years.

I very much regret having to bring up the subject I wish to bring up at all, and I particularly regret having to bring it up at this time towards the end of the session. However, I have tried every other method, and I have really no choice but to raise the matter before the committee. This case involves a rather elderly lady who suffered, I think, a great injustice at the hands of some of the officials of the Department of Public Works. This is an example of what I would describe as a disgraceful form of bureaucracy, and I wish to bring it to the attention of the minister, his parliamentary secretary and the members of the committee. I might add, Mr. Chairman, that I have already brought this matter to the attention of the minister and his parliamentary secretary but I should like to do so again.
I have a number of letters here and I had intended to read them into the record. However, in order to save time I shall paraphrase it. This case concerns a Mrs. Olive Showier of the city of Woodstock, Ontario who, on February 15 last, when entering a federal building in the city of Woodstock, slipped and fell on the icy steps causing some damage to her knee. Apparently that evening the caretaker-and this reminds me of the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West as to the difficulty in ascertaining who is in charge of these buildings-came around to see the good lady and take note of her injury. He instructed her to do certain things. In a letter directed to me dated May 1 last, Mrs. Showier wrote as follows:
The accident was reported to the post office February 15 and Mr. McCutcheon-
Presumably the caretaker.
-was speaking to my niece over the phone that evening.
On Saturday February 16, Mr. McCutcheon came down to the house to see me between one and two o'clock p.m. He admitted there had been

salt put on the steps that morning, but it does not melt the ice as quickly on the north side of the street.
Mr. McCutcheon called again at the house February 19 and asked me to write three letters explaining how the accident happened for him to forward to the complaint department which I did and he picked them up the same evening.
Then, she goes on to mention another matter concerning her out-of-pocket expenses which amounted to $20.50. This is all the good lady is asking. There was some correspondence between me and the minister and his parliamentary secretary.
I only wish to read one letter which was sent to me from the minister on June 21, 1963. I realize the minister did not write it himself. It was drawn up by some of his officials and it is a masterpiece of what I call red tape and eyewash. It reads:
Dear Mr. Nesbitt:
This refers to our recent exchange of correspondence about Mrs. Showler's unfortunate accident on the steps of the Woodstock federal building.
As the director of our property and building management branch pointed out to Mrs. Showier, her claim cannot be considered because it was not submitted within seven days of the date of the accident, as required by the Crown Liability Act. Other requirements of the act must also be met. Such notice must be served upon a responsible official of this department and a copy of the notice must be sent by registered mail to the deputy attorney general. This does not appear to have been done in this case.
Notwithstanding the disqualification of her claim because of the time factor and the lack of official notice, there is no evidence of negligence on the part of the crown. The steps were cleared of ice and snow, and salted at 3.15 p.m. Mrs. Showier reported that she fell at 3.45 p.m. At that time, the steps were reported to be clear, but wet.
Bear this in mind.
A medical certificate dated February 19, 1963, on our file, reports that Mrs. Showier did not suffer any serious injury as a result of her fall.
Mrs. Showler's claim that Mr. McCutcheon told her the steps were, in fact, icy has been investigated. It does not appear, after verification of this point with Mr. McCutcheon, caretaker of the building, that such a statement was ever made to Mrs. Showier.
I'll bet it wasn't, after the verification was made.
Also, Mr. McCutcheon's suggestion to Mrs. Showier that she submit a claim should not be interpreted as an admission of negligence. It is simply a courtesy extended to persons in such cases in the interests of justice and fair play.
In these circumstances, it appears that the department exercised all reasonable care and precaution, that the accident was not due to any negligence on the part of a servant of the crown, and that therefore, there is no legal liability on the part of the crown.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question. When did this occur?

It occurred last February 15 and the correspondence went on last June and July.
Supply-Public Works
Then the Conservatives were in office at that time. Why didn't they settle the problem?

If it is of any interest to the hon. member the point was not brought to the attention of the department then. The first correspondence was on May 7, 1963, if that satisfies my hon. friend, who seems interested in disturbing the lady's claim.
This is one of the most offensive cases I have seen in the ten years or so I have been a member of parliament. I realize the minister must have many complaints and cannot personally look into them all, but this is a particularly unfortunate case. The lady is still suffering. She is still using a crutch. She is not seeking any permanent damages from the department and only asks that she receive out-of-pocket expenses of $20.50 for an X-ray.
Someone may ask, why is all this time being wasted in bringing up the claim of an elderly lady in Woodstock for $20? But, as has been said, this is a court of last resort. I fully agree with the hon. member for Port Arthur that if an ombudsman were functioning it would not be necessary for members of parliament to bring up such things, but until such an institution is brought into effect the ordinary citizen has absolutely no recourse against some of the procedures followed in some government departments, except to have their member of parliament bring the matter up in this house.
It is my contention that this lady has been very unfairly treated. I have talked to her on several occasions and I have no doubt at all her story is absolutely true. I think the correspondence I have read into the record will verify that, and I hope the minister will give this matter further consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I want to talk tonight about Three Rivers and its famous bridge. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) must be just as interested as I am to see carried out that gigantic project which has been firing the imagination of the people of Three Rivers for more than 60 years. I appeal to the Minister of Public Works so that he will use his influence-and he is very influential, I think-with the government in order to settle, once and for all, that utterly ridiculous situation which is highly detrimental to the whole of central Quebec.
It must be remembered that it is a bridge which would connect the two shores of the St. Lawrence; it would be the only one between Montreal and Quebec city, which are 180 miles apart, to serve a population of about 250,000 people.
When I was minister of transport, I had the opportunity to study this question thoroughly with the engineers of my department and

Supply-Public Works
those of the Department of Public Works. We discussed it with the directors of the corporation, which is an independent corporation, created by the Quebec government, in which there are representatives of all parties, but mostly of the Liberal party.
So, I had the opportunity to study this question thoroughly and even organize meetings with the corporation of the Three Rivers bridge and the engineers of the provincial government. We considered all suggestions and there was never any mention of an expenditure of $60 million, nor of $30 million, not even of $10 million; mention was always made of an expenditure of $5 to $7 million. The engineers of the Department of Public Works had reached the conclusion that the federal government would be likely to pay an amount of $5 to $7 million in order to protect navigation on the St. Lawrence.
Mr. Chairman, I am told it is ten thirty. I would like to know whether it is the intention of the house to sit a little longer tonight.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is that agreed?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, when we opened the negotiations with the representatives of the provincial government and those of the corporation of the Three Rivers bridge, the latter proposed that a bridge be built on a site which had been approved by the former minister of transport, Mr. Marler. There is no doubt that the construction of a bridge at that place could have interfered with navigation on the St. Lawrence and could have impeded the flow of ice on the river. Consequently, as minister of transport, I got in touch with the head of the corporation and the provincial authorities and I asked them to consider other alternatives.
That is how it was later proposed to build the bridge between the municipality of St. Angele, opposite Three Rivers, and St. Quentin island. If the project had been carried out at that place, it would not have cost a cent to the federal government; however, it would have involved an expenditure of $10 to $12 million for the provincial government and the city of Three Rivers. The bridge would have been built right between the town of Cap de la Madeleine and Three Rivers. It would have had to pass under the Duplessis bridge and would have necessitated the construction of another one on the east side of the St. Maurice and a third one over that river. There is no doubt that the project would have cost at least $10 to $12 million to the provincial government. Now, as the provincial government had given a statutory 
guarantee for the expenses of the corporation and since the cost of the bridge could reach something like $35 million, the province indicated to us that it could go no further.
That is why I feel that the federal government would be justified to provide $5 to $7 million for the construction of a bridge for the benefit not only of the local residents, but of all the people in the province of Quebec. That expenditure would help the economic and industrial development not only of the centre of the province of Quebec, but of the whole of Canada.
Work has started. The bridge corporation has hired engineers who, for the last 12 months or so, have been busy with their engineering work; the corporation expropriated the necessary land, and last week, it obtained from the provincial government a first loan of $1,180,000. The corporation officials have announced that tenders for the first stages of the work would be called in the very first days of January 1964.
Mr. Chairman, one can well imagine the feelings of the population of Three Rivers when they heard the new Minister of Transport state, that according to his experts, the order in council signed on March 4 of last year was not legal, or at least, that its legality was open to question. This is absolutely ridiculous, for everyone knows that once signed by the governor general, an order in council cannot be cancelled, as it is absolutely legal. If the government thinks that Three Rivers is not entitled to a bridge, let it take its responsibilities; let it issue a new order in council and deprive the population of that region of this very necessary bridge.
The Minister of Transport does not want to take his responsibilities; for more than a month and a half, we have been urging him to tell us whether the government intends to cancel everything which was done under the former government to carry out that ambitious program. The minister beats about the bush, gives vague answers and refuses to tell us what stand the federal government intends to take. It is quite clear that he creates all sorts of obstacles to stop the building of a bridge which is absolutely necessary to the development of that part of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the Minister of Public Works, who is responsible for this, to have works carried out in the St. Lawrence river to protect the bridge against the ice, to control floods and help navigation. I ask him to take his responsibilities too, to co-operate with the bridge corporation and the provincial government, so that this ridiculous situation may be settled once and for all.

Mr. Chairman, today, in a reply to a question put by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), the Minister of Transport said that surveys had been made on the St. Lawrence river since last March.
This afternoon, I asked the Minister of Public Works whether surveys had been made in his department concerning the construction of dikes on lake St. Pierre. He answered no. Maybe my question was not clear enough-
No survey was made by the Department of Public Works. That is what 1 meant.

I would ask the Minister of Public Works to take his responsibilities once and for all and to help the Minister of Transport to extricate himself from all those difficulties which are his own doing.
Mr. Chairman, I thank the house for having been so kind as to let me have the floor so long.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief. I simply wish to ask some information of the Minister of Public Works, concerning the St. Charles river project, in Quebec.
I know a delegation from Quebec met the minister in that respect, about a month ago. I should like to ask the minister what are the immediate projects concerning that river and the agreements reached or the arrangements made with the authorities of the city of Quebec, concerning the development of the St. Charles river, in Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, since this item deals with the appropriation for dredging I would like to make a very brief reference to a condition which exists in my constituency. It is with respect to the water level of lake Winnipegosis. I would like to refer to the amount of money the government is spending each year on dredging this lake. I am advised by the department that they have spent approximately $47,000 a year during the last seven years, which gives a total amount in excess of $310,000.
I would suggest to the minister that he could save his department a considerable sum of money over the next few years by the construction of a dam on the West Waterhen river to maintain the water level of the lake. At the present time it is just impossible for the dredge crew to clear channels fast enough to serve the industries on the lake. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I would like to place on the record a letter I have received from the Winnipegosis chamber of commerce outlining the drastic situation which has developed:
Supply-Public Works
The Winnipegosis chamber of commerce wishes to place before you the drastic situation the village of Winnipegosis and the surrounding areas are confronted with due to the low level of lake Winnipegosis. The residents of Winnipegosis are dependent on income coming from four sources, namely, lumber, fish, cattle and tourist. All four are in one way or another dependant on the water level of lake Winnipegosis.
In the past years an income of approximately $150,000 was obtained from lumbering alone. All the lumber was transported on the lake to the town of Winnipegosis. Due to a terrific drop in water level this will soon be an impossibility. Second, the value of fish caught in lake Winnipegosis reached $956,023 in 1961. This catch is going down and to our understanding this industry will soon discontinue, mainly caused by low water level. Cattle ranchers from Salt Point are dependant on the lake for transportation of their beef to Winnipegosis. They hope that some dredging would soon be done in order to be able to load and ship their cattle. When the water had been higher, dredging was not necessary. In other places cattle cannot reach the waterline due to long stretches of muck into which they sink while trying to get a drink. In the winter, because of low level, the water freezes to the bottom, and once again ranchers are faced with a problem. To overcome this, we know of ranchers paying high prices to welldiggers but cannot reach water on land.
Let us now turn to the tourist trade. Angling on lake Winnipegosis will soon be a thing of the past. Many fishing and hunting lodges are not accessible any more by boats. When you come to the lakeshore, all you can see are stretches of muck with some ducks beyond that. This will soon affect the duck population about which we are concerned, especially the redheads which make lake Winnipegosis their best breeding grounds...
We must state once again that we are faced with a critical situation which, to our understanding and belief, can be corrected by a dam on the West Waterhen river.
Hoping that you will give our plea your utmost consideration and give us some assurance that our problem will soon be corrected.
Since Dauphin is the only place in Manitoba declared a designated area, the construction of the dam would give employment to a great number of people this winter. To indicate the responsibility of the federal government in the matter, the Minister of Labour has interpreted a "designated area" as follows, and I will just quote in part from an answer he gave to a question by the hon. member for Churchill:
This area will also qualify in connection with the supplementary federal government winter construction program, which applies to designated development areas and designated areas of high winter unemployment.
If the government are serious with regard to creating employment in a designated area, then I suggest that the construction of such a dam on the Waterhen river this winter, besides giving employment to a great number of people living in the area would help to maintain, as pointed out in the letter, the fishing industry, the lumbering industry, the cattle industry and it would help to conserve our wildlife, as well as the important tourist industry.

Supply-Public Works
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister to give this matter his most serious consideration with a view to getting the project under way in the very near future. [Translation]
Mr. Chairman, my first words are to express my admiration for the Minister of Public Works. I thank him for all he has done and for the courtesy-
If the hon. member has so much admiration for the minister, it would be preferable to vote his credits.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I object to what the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has just said. If ever a member has wasted the time of the house, it is the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments I feel I should make concerning the estimates of the Department of Public Works.
Taking a look at the estimates of this department for the year 1962-63, we find that they have been cut from $191 million to $178 million. Everyone knows how urgent it is that work be carried out to deal with unemployment. The minister, despite his good intentions, remains incapable of solving this problem with the small amount of money made available to him. He can only tell us that he has not got a penny left and it is impossible for him to consider any new requests until next year.
On the other hand, I find that national defence takes up 25.6 per cent of our national budget; the Department of National Health and Welfare, 19.1 per cent; debt charges, 13.5 per cent, that we have to pay in interests; payments to the provinces, 3.3 per cent -I approve of this expenditure and I know it will increase-veterans' affairs, 5.3 per cent; transport, 4 per cent; public works, only 2.8 per cent.
If there is one department whose estimates should be increased, it is the public works department, which must undertake huge works where they are needed. Instead of investing money in public works, the government prefers to leave families in such abject poverty that 19.1 per cent of the national budget has to be affected to the Department of National Health and Welfare.
We are not against giving help to families in need but we all admit that if a greater number of public works were undertaken, there would not be so many of them. In my riding, many farmers get help from the welfare department. They are no longer able to earn a living from their farms. There are also a great number of workers, in the cities, who

live on social welfare. They look for jobs but they cannot find any because no public works are undertaken.
In my opinion, this government should direct its activities towards public works, particularly if it wants to alleviate the unemployment situation.
I admit that will only partially meet our problems. A great many citizens are only too anxious to have work.
In the riding of Megantic, where I live, we have a splendid city planning project which is admired by many people from abroad, especially Americans who visit us. We could welcome a great number of tourists. It would be and important incentive to our town and to all our county to find in the tourist industry an important livelihood for our families. Besides, one knows that where the government spends $3, it brings in more than six.
Mr. Chairman, we have great projects to carry out. In this connection, by improving waterways, lakes, etc., as needed, we could give plenty to work to many people.
However, there is not only the water areas that might be improved. It is true that there is a magnificent lake in my own city, and such lakes are not to be found in every town.
Finally throughout my constituency, people wonder what the federal government is doing about public works. They wonder whether the government invests money only along lakes and waterways. In several parishes of my riding, people cannot take advantage of public works. All kinds of suggestions are being made to us with a request to submit them to the government in order to help the citizens of my riding.
One can find in my constituency many abandoned farms where there is almost nothing left. The farms have been deserted. We are being asked to proceed to the reafforestation of those lands and, to do so, we are being asked to see the Minister of Public Works who, by extending the winter works period until May, for example, or until June, could rehabilitate those fertile and abandoned pieces of land. In view of the fact that many farmers having private properties are unable to do such a thing, the Department of Public Works could employ unemployed people in my constituency in order to undertake the reafforestation of those lands. Besides, according to federal and provincial engineers, reafforestation would be an ideal solution for the rehabilitation of those lands.
We are also asked to request the Minister of Public Works to build dams on the many lakes of that area.
I would also like to point out to the minister the damages owing to drought prevalent in

my constituency in summertime. There should be an irrigation system and dams should be erected on lakes so as to regulate spring water and provide water all year round.
Moreover, in co-operation with the provincial government, we are asked to urge the Department of Public Works to build fish hatcheries to breed fish for restocking lakes. These lakes have been fished out, and tourists are no longer interested to visit them. It would therefore be necessary to launch all kinds of public works.
Thus, the winter works program could be used to improve level crossings which are quite numerous in my riding, especially in the populated areas. That is where improvements are necessary. However, nothing can be done because no funds are available. Yet, if there was money, it would be possible to provide work for the unemployed and improve those level crossings.
Numerous other means have been suggested to us, but I could not list them all tonight because that would take too much time. As I do not wish to delay the committee, I shall not insist on that point.
I would therefore ask the Department of Public Works to give serious consideration to those cases and to provide more funds to correct such anomalies.
In considering the estimates of the Department of Public Works, I find that the government allocates it only $178 million, when it should receive at least $400 million. The national defence estimates should be reduced by several million dollars to use them in the Department of Public Works. If that were done, the government would be in a better position to really do something for the country and the welfare of its citizens, not to mention that this will also develop Canada further.

I have in mind the question of residence, particularly with respect to old age security but also with respect to the others. One of the complaints that seems to have come to me from a great many people in recent months is that of elderly people who have lived in Canada perhaps 40, 50 or 60 years, but who have had to go elsewhere because of health, and find this one year requirement before they can qualify for the old age security pension a very difficult and awkward one to meet. [The Chairman.]

With respect to the disability definition 1 agree with my friend that it is a rather restrictive one and a number of hon. members have already mentioned this, as indeed I did when I was on the other side of the house.
